A.21. Executive summary (max 750 words; approximately 4 pages)

Climate Change Problem

Colombia's landscape is facing a period of unprecedented ecological and climate-related challenges. The country undertakes an ambitious transformation to meet its Nationally Determined Contribution, among the most ambitious in Latin America. As one of the most disaster affected countries on earth, Colombia faces significant risks from climate change. The conservation and sustainable use of Amazon forests are a critical global carbon sink, both highly impacted by increasing climate variability and projected changes in precipitation patterns leading to global warming.

Observations and future projected changes in climate under RCP 4.5 show increasing temperatures and greater variability in precipitation patterns, leading to an increased incidence of droughts, flooding, landslides, and fires, negatively affecting ecosystems nationwide. Water provisioning and regulation are critically impacted by climate change. Unreliable water distribution, coupled with varying

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V3.0 | PAGE 3

A

demand, and is extremely low water availability in some areas and excesses in others that cause significant periodic flooding. The National Water Study estimates that almost 50% of the urban population is vulnerable to drought on an average year, while this proportion may increase to reach up to 80% during dry years. *Rain* is common and agricultural land use has been expanded into areas that are especially vulnerable to changes in climate.

3. Meanwhile, after having endured five decades of armed conflict with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), which signed a peace agreement in 2016, the country is confronting a new wave of deforestation and significant alterations of terrestrial socio-ecological systems, leading to increased GHG emissions and reduced carbon sequestration. The Colombian government has committed itself to improving water provisioning. Nowhere are these pressures more pronounced and complex than in and around Colombia’s National System of Protected Areas (SNAP), which is the largest network of protected areas in Latin America and a global biodiversity hotspot, providing critical havens for biodiversity and critical nature-based solutions to the climate crisis. As highlighted in a recent report by WWF Colombia, the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development (MADS) has committed 39 PA’s in the country (7%) with increased or decreased forested areas in the years following the peace accord.

4. Land use change and climate impacts are two determinant factors of sustainable water yield, and data clearly indicates that Colombia will be unable to sustain the hydrological functionality of its watersheds in a changing climate without safeguarding forest ecosystems in key protected areas. Colombia’s SNAP covers 15% of the country’s total land area (20 million hectares), which is larger than the size of all PA’s in the country’s total surface area, 50% of the hydro-energy produced in Colombia uses water provided by these watersheds, and 70% of the population relies on rivers for drinking water. The SNAP provides drinking water for more than 25 million people, for an estimated annual value of US$ 491 million*, while the FAD provides drinking water to approximately 38 million people in Colombia, with an average daily consumption per capita of 70 liters (compared to a global average of 60 liters and a Colombian average year*). An analysis of water provisioning during average and dry years for the five hydrographic basins that supply the FAD shows that the SNAP provides approximately 15% more water than the FAD, and 30% additional water available as compared to those sub-basins without national parks*. Yet, the connectivity of the system is limited, the effectiveness of current management is low, maintaining the network has been challenging due to lack of resources, and the capacity for climate change adaptation in the SNAP is clearly inadequate.

5. SNAP’s new 2020-30 policy*, approved by the National Protected Areas Commission (CONAP) in May 2019, seeks to change those trends, as do local and national peacebuilding initiatives implemented under the territorial peace approach* as part of the peace agreement. Although the Colombian government has committed itself to improving water provisioning, it is clear that the current management capacity of the system still faces a significant financial gap to achieve the ambitions of the NDC and SNAP 2030 policy goals. The proposed project will address this gap by providing technical assistance in three key categories: (1) Access to Finance: the capacity of key territorial entities to access and sequence existing and new funding sources for the implementation of the SNAP 2030 policy; (2) Capacity Building: Management of integrated landscapes of PA’s and adjacent private lands in the ecological area of influence of the PA, specifically as it relates to limited capacities to develop and implement land-based sustainable landscape management and climate change adaptation strategies.

Proposed approach

6. The proposed project will commission WWF’s regional vision and strategy for the Amazon, which will bring together Global Finance for Protection (GFP)* projects in Brazil, Peru, and Colombia under WWF’s Earth for Life initiative. Together, these three country initiatives will secure the long-term protection of approximately 13% of the Amazon biome, and foster a paradigm shift towards low-emission and climate-resilient landscapes.

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V3.0 | PAGE A

## Project Description and Objectives

### Background on the Project

1. Since 2015, WWF has been supporting the use of the PPF methodology through Heritage Colombia (HECO), a public-private partnership designed to secure financial sustainability for large-scale landscape management projects in Colombia.
2. The project aims to reduce deforestation and forest degradation by promoting sustainable land-use practices that align with national policies and international commitments.

### Project Components

3. The two landscapes targeted in this GCF project will conserve 8,6 million ha, representing one third of the total 20 billion ha goal, and more than 5.8% of Colombia's territory.
4. These landscapes include both protected areas (already designated or expected to be included in the system of national, sub-national, and local protected areas) and ecologically connected priority areas for biodiversity conservation.

### Project Goals

5. The project’s goal is to realize a new paradigm of sustainable landscape finance that combines climate change mitigation with ecosystem services provision, including carbon sequestration and storage, water regulation, and generating provisions in a changing climate.
6. Three complementary components have been designed to contribute to the achievement of this goal: i) financial mechanisms for scaling up project implementation; ii) institutional arrangements and implementation; iii) participatory monitoring systems that generate climate information used for decision-making.

### Similar Projects

7. Similar to the PPF in Bhutan for Life (GCF FP050), this project is designed to address structural funding gaps by providing a financial mechanism for scaling up project implementation, including government investments significantly above baselines during a short-term financial transition period.
8. The project will leverage $12 million of GCF funds over 3 years and $102 million in additional investment from WWF, the Government of Colombia, and various philanthropic donors.

### Project Impact

9. Project interventions will bring $7.2 million under climate-resilient management practices and directly benefit 329,658 people from increased capacity for using climate information, managing climate risks on their land, and participating in adaptation planning.
10. The project will also implement Adaptation Interactions that protect and maintain ecosystems that provide water regulation to supply large urban populations.

### Mitigation Impact

11. The total mitigation impact from reduced deforestation, forest restoration, and preserved sinks corresponds to 8.9 million tCO2eq at project completion (10 years) and 46.3 million tCO2eq cumulatively.

# B. PROJECT PROGRAMME INFORMATION

## A. Context (max. 1000 words, approximately two pages)

### Country context

Colombia is the third most populous country in Latin America with >51.5 million people* with a GIDP of US$271 billion (World Bank, 2019). The poverty rate stands at 34%, while 12% of the population lives in extreme poverty and 18.1% in multidimensional poverty for 2020.* Agriculture, livestock and aquaculture represent 7.6% of the GDP at national level (World Bank, 2019). The agricultural sector is a major source of income; small-scale properties are cultivated by 80% of the rural population and represent 25% of the total area, while their production was estimated between 50% and 68% of total agricultural production.

#### Ecosystems and Ecosystem Services

The majority of Colombia's ecosystems have been identified in Colombia.* Experts estimate that 66% of their original area remains, although there is significant variation regarding human intervention. Due to the concentration of the population in urban areas and the expansion of agriculture and livestock activities, most of the country’s ecosystems have been transformed, with only 42% and 32% of their original cover remaining, respectively.*


#### Water provisioning and regulation are without a doubt Colombia's most important ecosystem services. The country has an extensive network of rivers and lakes that provide water for human consumption and irrigation. However, the majority of these environments show evidence of some degree of transformation caused by urbanization, agriculture expansion, cattle ranching, deforestation, and other activities. According to the National Hydrographic Network (NHN), 20% of the country's territory corresponds to the agricultural (53.1%), energy (24.3%), and domestic use (17.1%) sectors. According to the same source, 68% of the rivers are used for irrigation purposes. The remaining 19% is dedicated to other uses. These functions provided by the country's nearly 3 million hectares of high mountain ("paramo") ecosystems, including sediment control and filtration, erosion control and landslide and flood risk reduction and support for most of the water resources in the country. However, the transformation of these environments has led to a significant decrease in their functions, resulting in extremely low water availability in some areas and excesses in others that cause significant periodic flooding. The loss of these ecosystems also results in a significant decline in biodiversity, as well as the degradation of pastures, forests, paramos, and wetlands provide essential flow regulation and flood risk reduction benefits to human populations.

### Current climatic conditions

A detailed climate analysis and methodology is presented in Annex 2: Feasibility Study. The information provided in this document is based on the results obtained from the Climate Atlas of Colombia (2015). Due to the complex geography of the country, the following descriptions of climate patterns and current impacts of climate change are limited to five main project implementation regions (mocasías*) with more detailed examples provided on each and every one.

#### 17. Climate variation in Colombia is largely determined by the complex topography of its continental territory. Due to its geographical location in the northwestern corner of South America close to the equator, climate is also strongly influenced by oceanic currents.

## GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V3.0 | PAGE B

### Influenced by the winds and the southern oscillation of the intertropical convergence zone, The El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) events, which tend to occur every 3 to 7 years, strongly modify the rainfall patterns throughout the country. As a rule, El Niño events cause La Niña events and an increase in temperature, especially in the eastern part of Colombia.

18. In the equatorial zone, the amount of solar energy varies minimally throughout the year, which explains the minimal monthly variation of air temperature, ranging from 1 to 3°C. However, the thermal regime in Colombia has a more marked seasonal rhythm than that of other tropical countries due to its geographical location and altitude among other factors. For instance, both in the Pacific and Amazon regions, evapotranspiration contributes to lessen the amplitude of the diurnal temperature range, which is greater in areas where mean air temperature is higher than 32°C, and others where mean temperature is just a few degrees above 0°C.

19. The north-eastern extreme of the Caribbean region, in the Departments of La Guajira, Atlántico and Cesar, is influenced by the trade winds from the northeast, which are responsible for the high rainfall recorded there. In this portion of the Colombian Caribbean, annual rainfall reaches 300-600 mm, but to the south, as the lowlands yield to the mountains, it increases up to 1500 mm.

Rainfall distribution along the year is bimodal: the first rainy season occurs from mid-April until early June and the second, more intense period, from early September to late December. Most localities around the Caribbean region have a dry season between April and October. The exception is the Guajira peninsula and along the Cesar River valley. The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta has a different thermal regime than that of the rest of the country.

20. San Lucas is a transitional zone between the semi-arid conditions of the southern Caribbean lowlands and most of foothills of the northern Central Andes. Mean temperature in the area is 28.2°C (12-35°C), although it may reach up to 40°C during the dry season, especially at midday. The annual rainfall ranges from 600 mm to 900 mm and the rainy season occurs during the first quarter (January-March) when there is a water deficit in the soil. Between April and October, the area experiences a dry season.

21. Due to the complex topography of the Andean region, rainfall variation is considerable and depends on a number of factors including exposure, orientation of the slopes, and elevation. In general, annual rainfall is lower (reaching less than 1,200 mm) at the bottom of the upper Magdalena valley (Huila), upper Cauca valley (Valle del Cauca), and in some localities on the eastern side of the Central Andes. The highest rainfall occurs in the western slopes of the central Andes, where annual precipitation reaches 2,000-4,000 mm. Rainfall is bimodal, although seasonal occurrence of dry and wet seasons varies latitudes. The first rainy season begins from mid-April until early June and the second more severe rainy season begins towards the end of September and lasts up to late December.

Rainfall bands are well defined along the elevation gradient. The highest mean temperatures (24-28°C) are found in the dry valleys of the upper Magdalena valley, Cauca, Sugamuxi and Páipa, while in the Andean plateaus of Centralamerica, Boyacá and Norte and the mountains of Antioquia, Caucás and the coffee growing region, mean temperatures are between 12 and 16°C.

### Observed climate changes

The information presented below includes key results from the analysis (see detailed analysis and methodology in Annex 2) to support the project's climatic rationale. Observed historical data shows the significant increase of rainfall during El Niño events, which is consistent with the findings by other authors who followed it between 1991, 1998 and 2004. The first two years with the highest rainfall in the country coincide with those of the strongest El Niño events (1997-1998) and the second strongest event (1982-1983). On the other hand, the El Niño years with the lowest rainfall in the country during the period 1970-2011 were 1997, 1998 and 2004. The most severe droughts occurred between 1996 and 2003, which coincided with La Niña related disasters per year. According to the National Office for Disaster Risk Management (UNIDR), rainfall-related disasters increased by 15.1% from 1990-2017, especially during periods of La Niña. The IPCC estimates that

# Projected climate change

The information presented below includes key results from the analysis developed to support the project’s climate risk assessment (CRS 4.5 with some figures also showing CRS 4.5 for comparative purposes), supplemented by data from the 2017 National Communication (NC) of Colombia under the UNFCCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change). The magnitude of extreme rainfall occurrences is rising across all mosaics. Climate change projections indicate a rise in annual average rainfall, with an increase of up to 5% by the end of the century. This is accompanied by an increase and decrease in the number of colder averages. Overall annual rainfall is expected to rise by 0.8 to 1.6 percent, with some mosaics showing increases as high as 24%. The projected increase in average temperature will be between 3% and 5%, and there has also been an increase in the frequency of severe rainfall days (Figure 6).

## Rainfall

Rainfall in Colombia is highly varied spatially and strongly topographically controlled. The highest rainfall occurs in the Andes, with a decrease towards the north and east. The lowest rainfall occurs in the northwest to southwest coastal areas and the Andes range. The projected future (2050) sees an increase in rainfall along the western coast and the eastern interior of the country. There are areas to the south and far north that remain unchanged or see decreases. This pattern is also seen for the period 2100.

Both the Caribbean and San Lucas areas show long term variability in total rainfall but no distinct trend in either direction.* These areas are near the transition zones between increasing and decreasing rainfall. There is, however, a slight increase in rainfall from May to August in the San Lucas area. In the Caribbean, there is an increase in rainfall during January and February. Both locations see a decrease in monthly rainfall from August to December.

Orosho Transition and Central Andes areas are in the increasing precipitation area and these areas see an increase of between 5 and 20% by the end of the century. These increases are noted in the peak period of May and June, with some areas also showing a decrease during September and October. The central Andes area is in the heart of the Amazon area and is also in the increasing precipitation area but closer to the transition. There is an increase of 5% – 10% annual rainfall in this area. This is due mostly to an increase between April and June in the peak period.

Currently, the longest dry spells are in the north with ~30–50 days. The projected future (2050) sees longer dry spells (>2 days) in the far south-east in the area where there is a projected decrease in total rainfall; this is enhanced by an increase of 10% to 20% annual rainfall and a decrease in the number of colder averages. There is also a higher chance of the dry spell duration in the coastal western areas. The seasonal change in dry days is very different in the Caribbean and San Lucas areas, with the former seeing a decrease from May to August and an increase during September to November which is generally outside of the rainfall period.

## Variability

Rainfall variability is highest in the far northern areas and the central-eastern areas of the country. The more southern and western areas see a lower year on year variability meaning rainfall is more predictable and has a lower standard deviation (SD) than other areas. This is also reflected by the number of colder averages, with fewer cold days to the north and to the northwest Pacific coast. The remaining areas see an increase in total variability of up to 13% in the far northern areas.

The Caribbean mosaic is located in a region of Colombia with increasing variability, with an anticipated increase in the standard-deviation of up to 200 mm/year. The majority of this is due to variability in June–July August (JJA). San Lucas lies on the interface between increasing and decreasing variability areas see variability between 15% and 30%. This area also shows a projected future change in annual average rainfall by 2050, while the 2017 National Communication projective decrease of up to 40 mm/year. The San Lucas mosaic is representative of all three localities as representative of all of these mosaics. Geographies are also distinct; with the 2017 NC analysis pertaining to a larger area than the CRS 4.5 analysis.

### The Central Andes sees a wide decrease of variability between -5- and 65mm annually with MAM, JJA and SON all showing reduced variability. The Heart of the Amazon is varied in the seasonal response with MAM showing increased variability while JJA has seen either side of the change and DJF and JJA both showing increased variability but with a narrower range.

### Temperature

#### 32. **The hottest areas of the country are in the lower-lying eastern area and to the far north, with the higher altitude Andes region experiencing lower temperatures. Projected changes to maximum temperatures see an increase in the south and eastern areas of the country by 2.9–4.0°C. The northeastern coastal area sees the lowest changes, with a projected increase of only 1.5-3.0°C.** In the central Andes region, the average temperature is expected to be 31±0.8°C by 2021 and 32±0.4°C by RCP6.0 by the end of the century. The cooler areas of Caribe, Orinoco Transition and Central Andes increase from 18.2±1 to 20.5 ±2°C under RCP4.5. This is exacerbated further under the RCP8.5 scenario.

#### 34. **The minimum temperatures which are lowest in the elevated Andes areas are projected to increase in the future. These increases are likely most notable to the south and northeast of the country. Again, the western coastal region sees a lower increase than other regions with an average increase from 10±0.5°C by 2021 to 13±0.8°C under RCP6.0. The central Andes area is projected to see a decrease in temperature of -40% to -55% toward the end of the century. The coastal area is the exception to this which sees an increase from 9±0.2°C by 2021 to 13±0.8°C under RCP6.0.**

### Impacts of climate change

#### Observed climate change impacts

**35. Colombia is vulnerable to extreme weather impacts due to the high recurrence and magnitude of disasters associated with El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycles and decadal variability of El Niño La Niña South Oscillation (ENSO) cycles and changing climate conditions. The climate change parameters noted are already worsening these extremes, and future changes will likely exacerbate them further.** Colombia is projected to experience more frequent and intense extreme weather events in the coming decades, with a higher frequency of short-term hazards such as droughts, flooding, landslides, and fires, negatively affecting agriculture, water resources, infrastructure, ecosystems, and human health.

#### 36. **Hazards of extreme weather are also increasingly affecting ecosystems, livelihoods, infrastructure, and the larger economy in all project geographies, with flooding, drought, landslides, and fires all increasing in recent decades (Table 1). The projected increase in frequency and intensity of these hazards is expected to cost Colombia as much as 1.5% annually of Colombian GDP by the 2030 annual growth rate damage costs.** The Ministry of the Environment estimates 2% of the total population will be affected by floods in 2030, representing 2.2% of the GDP. These hazards are projected to increase in all project geographies and include flooding in the Pacific Coast, the Caribbean Central Andes, Orinoco Transition, and flooding in the Heart of the Amazon (Table 1). The observed trends suggest that the projects’ target mosaics and the impacts thereof continue to show an increasing trend (Figure 5 and Table 2).

The northern areas of Caribe and San Lucas see an increase in mean annual rainfall (index) to a drier state.

43. Extreme rainfall and flooding causing damage to property and road infrastructure, while landslides and mudslides, worsened by poor urban design and deforestation, can endanger human populations. Runoff levels in rivers and streams increase, impacting water availability. The likelihood of natural catastrophes, Salinity intrusion from sea-level rise can disrupt trade and destroy communities, impacting the lives and well-being of millions of Colombians living along the coast.

44. While changes in precipitation patterns in Colombia are expected to differ by area, there are also key similarities across all areas that are already affecting the unusually high fluctuations in water availability in Colombia due to the ENSO


---
**Page 21**
---

cycles. Reductions in river runoff due to increasing temperatures and fewer rainy days would affect water storage in dams and aquifer recharge. Because the Magdalena River basin supplies 70% of Colombia's hydropower, energy output may be drastically curtailed. Reduced runoff will potentially jeopardize rural and municipal water sources. The decline in water availability could also lead to increased salinity in coastal areas inhabited by shrimp and mudshells. Rising sea levels will cause saltwater intrusion into coastal aquifers, severely depleting freshwater supplies.

Increased precipitation and temperature declines are predicted to lead to the loss of snow-covered regions as early as 2030.


45. Agriculture in Colombia is vulnerable to increased soil erosion and desertification as a result of increased climate variability, which includes both temperature increases and unpredictable rainfall. Some indicators show that by 2020, up to 70% of the country's agricultural land will be degraded, particularly in the Andean region, with high-value commodities such as tropical fruit, cocoa, bananas, and coffee being particularly vulnerable.


46. Increased La Niña events may increase the frequency of droughts, impacting water supply and agriculture output. A rise in extreme rainfall events might lead to flooding and landslides, causing agricultural and animal damage and loss of life.

47. Rising temperatures are expected to be more pronounced at higher elevations, endangering fragile and distinctive mountain ecosystems and hastening the rate of land degradation. This might also lead to the extinction of unique species like high-altitude flora and animals.


48. Vector-borne illnesses such as malaria and dengue fever will spread when rainfall intensifies and temperatures rise. The increase in temperature will allow mosquitoes to breed more rapidly, increasing their numbers. Higher temperatures could potentially contribute to the spread of waterborne illnesses via contaminated water supplies. Rising temperatures can also lead to an increase in the amount of ozone and other pollutants in the air, especially in Bogotá and Cali, which have high levels of pollution, raising the risk of respiratory illnesses and cardiovascular disease.


49. Shifting precipitation patterns and increasing temperatures will also have direct impacts on agriculture, shortening growing seasons and reducing yields. Studies show that a 10% reduction in precipitation as modeled for the Third National Communication of The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta National Park and its expansion to the north area of 45% and 25% would have significant direct impacts: the Andean moist forest, the sub-Andean moist forest, and the coastal wetlands are all at risk. These areas are home to a wide variety of species with unique species composition with such significant declines. In Chiriguaná National Park, for example, an essential water source would be lost in 2035 under RCP 4.5 and 8.5 respectively, indicating permanent loss as warming continues.


Vulnerability to climate change and adaptation needs


50. Colombia is highly sensitive to climate impacts, as a result of strong socioeconomic inequality and poverty (55% of the population lives below the poverty line) and a legacy of conflict that has displaced about 8 million people; b) its population uniquely and especially vulnerable to increasing weather extremes. Part of this vulnerability stems from the fact that 70% of Colombia's territory is rural, with 62% of the country's population subject to the Integral Rural Reform (IRR), in Spanish included in the peace agreement. Colombian communities and territories are particularly vulnerable because they have limited access to information on climate change and its vulnerability to the existing impacts and future risks of climate change. The majority of the national population is located in areas with high exposure to natural hazards, such as floods, landslides, droughts, and earthquakes. These mismatches between where water flows and populations live, increasing stress and scarcity, or expose to coastal


---
**Page 22**
---

storms and sea level rise on coastlines. These along with the related adaptation needs are described further below (additional detail is provided in Annex 2).

51. Existing high precipitation variability in many regions, defined by seasonal and interannual ENSO changes, resulting in enormous seasonal and interannual shifts in water flows and availability, from too much to too little, is a major challenge for Colombia's water resources management. The country has experienced a significant decrease in the increasing proportion of Colombia’s water supply is highly vulnerable to water deficits, scarcity, and reduced quality. This vulnerability is expected to increase by 2050 as the average annual precipitation decreases by approximately 13% on an average year, and that this proportion may increase to reach up to 80% during dry years. While Colombia has a large number of rivers, lakes, and reservoirs, most of these are located in remote areas where infrastructure is limited or non-existent. In addition, while the majority of the population lives in coastal regions, which have high precipitation levels, these areas also experience frequent flooding events.

52. Agricultural and subsistence-based livelihoods in poor and marginalized communities with often limited access to modern farming technology and basic infrastructure and services are highly dependent on ecosystem services. For example, in the Amazon region, 80% of the population depends directly or indirectly on forest resources for their livelihood, nationally, with losses as high as nearly 15% in some departments, as a result of reduced biomass in high altitude forests. In addition to this, the agricultural sector is highly vulnerable to climate change impacts. The agricultural sector has been affected by climate change across four intervention scenarios (data not available for San Lucas) are expected to suffer from significant changes in areas optimal for the production of different agricultural crops (see full report in Annex 2). In addition, the agricultural sector is highly dependent on water resources and land productivity and agriculture, with low projected changes for the Heart of Amazonia and the Central Andes, low-to-medium changes in the Caribbean and the Amazon mosaic, medium-to-high changes in the Orinoquia-Amazonia and Pacific regions, and high-to very high changes in the Orinoco-Amazonia and Pacific regions, and the lowest levels in municipalities located in the Central and Eastern Andes. These areas are characterized by a significant interaction with poverty and lack of institutional presence. Sensitivity and adaptive capacity are inextricably linked by how poverty and inequality affect a population’s capacity to cope with the negative impacts of increasing climate variability.

## Current Gradations of Deforestation and Land Use Change

### Drivers of Deforestation and Land Use Change

64. During the period from 1985 to 2017, deforestation was widespread throughout the country. **Historic annual forest loss at national scale is dynamic**, with the highest value observed in 2017 (with 219,552 ha deforested). Studies have shown that deforestation is driven by a complex interplay of factors related to economic development, social and policy, and - in the case of Colombia - the withdrawal of the FARC following the peace accords. Studies also show that deforestation has been associated with increased poverty, reduced access to basic services, lower economic income and have low or non-existent punishment. The main illegal activities contributing to the current paradigm of deforestation are agricultural expansion (including illegal crops), land grabbing, illegal mining, illegal logging.

57. According to Arias-Gavira et al., et al. (2021) analysis of deforestation dynamics using the system thinking approach, where Causal Loop Diagrams were used to identify drivers of deforestation at national and regional scales, interaction between three main reinforcing loops: 1) Available areas for non-sustainable land activities (agriculture, livestock, and mining expansion); 2) Areas available for legal activities (cocoa, mining, timber extraction; and), 3) Urgent infrastructure that will keep increasing the demand of agricultural activities. The three reinforcing causal loop could slow down and stop deforestation are determined by governance schemes (sustainable territorial management) and other institutional mechanisms for conservation. **Detailed driver assessment results for each project geography are included**.

68. Deforestation and forest degradation have been shown to be interrelated as deforestation progresses, degraded forests become more vulnerable to further degradation. Land use change, particularly deforestation and resource conversion, contributes significantly to increased risk of landslides and flooding as they increase run-off, sediment deposition, and soil instability.

## Background and Context

The Green Climate Fund (GCF) has a baseline of US$ 8.2 million and requires an additional US$ 7.3 million annually. This figure does not account for necessary spending to address direct climate change impacts and risks, including strengthening infrastructure, new monitoring systems, training for project managers, and upscaling management plans to respond to the specific climate scenarios defined for each of the projects in this proposal.

### Heritage Colombia (HECO)

Since 2015, WWF has been supporting the use of the Project Finance for Permanence approach in Colombia through Heritage Colombia (HECO). HECO is a public-private partnership designed to secure financial resources and technical expertise from both sectors. The project aims to protect or restore over 20 million hectares over the next 20 years, led by the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development. This initiative has received significant political support through two administrations: first under President Santos and now under President Duque.

### Heritage Colombia GCF Project

The Heritage Colombia GCF project contributes to national climate mitigation and adaptation goals through three major components:

1. **Effective Management of Resilient Landscapes**: This component focuses on the Heart of the Andes and the Heart of the Amazon, in partnership with environmental authorities, local governments, indigenous communities, the private sector, and civil society. Heritage Colombia's mosaics were selected due to their level of vulnerability for climate change impacts.

2. **Effective Management of Resilient Landscapes**: This component focuses on Macarena and Chiriquite National Parks and their connectivity corridor with the highest climate change vulnerabilities (see Annex 2).

3. **Effective Management of Resilient Landscapes**: This component covers an area of 6.6 million ha, representing more than 5.8% of Colombia's territory. They include protected areas (national parks, natural parks, and national reserves), sub-national protected areas, and productive adjacent lands under other forms of tenure.

### Project Impact

Beyond these impacts, this GCF project will catalyze the Effective Management of an additional 23 million hectares, including 1.6 million hectares in PAAs and 7.7 million hectares in the broader mosaic. The GCF project's partners have committed to leveraging US$ 50 million from other sources through the Project Finance for Permanence (PFP) Management Framework through the PFP contract supported by the GCF, without additional GCF resources.

### Conclusion

The leverage from the GCF project, this integrated effort will ultimately yield 8.9 million hectares toward the Government of Colombia's vision to restore Heritage Colombia grassland, representing 60% of its total. The HECO GCF is targeted to close in 2022.

### B.2 (a). Theory of change narrative and diagram (max. 1500 words, approximately 3 pages plus diagram)

As highlighted in Section B.1, Colombia's landscapes and people are facing a period of unprecedented ecological challenges. The country is experiencing the largest deforestation rate globally, with forest loss linked to landscape restoration and reforestation projects coupled with efforts to reach net-zero deforestation by 2030 aimed at meeting its Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) under the Paris Agreement in 2015. *Compared to these trends*, as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic, global GDP fell by 6.8% in 2020, the largest contraction ever recorded.

To support this transformation, a new national policy focused on the consolidation of the SINAP 2020-2030 was adopted by the National Protected Areas Commission (CONAP) in May 2021 and officially launched by the president in October 2021. The new policy has five goals: (1) increased representation, (2) improved participatory governance, (3) enhanced ecosystem services and benefits, and (5) increased mainstreaming of climate sustainability for SINAP. All are hallmarks of the Effective Management approach.

Although the Colombian government has long demonstrated strong commitment to SINAP development and conservation, the country still faces a significant financial gap to achieve the ambitions of the NDC and SINAP 2030 policy goals. Without additional funding, the current SINAP implementation strategy will not be able to meet its objectives in terms of protected areas restrict the Effective Management of SINAP. The current paradigm limits the integration of climate change into management practices and hinders the surveillance and avoidance of illegal land uses, which continue to contribute significantly to deforestation. This is further exacerbated by the lack of financial resources (described in a number of challenges (described in FP Section B.2A) that have ultimately led to very low re-investment back into SINAP.

86. To revert land and water management in the mosaic towards a low carbon, climate resilient path, Colombia is implementing a new approach called the Project Finance for Permanence (PFP). The PFP approach is merged to conserve these strategic ecosystems and incentivize agricultural production with low impacts on forests. This innovative model seeks to address the lack of financial resources needed to protect areas and their buffer zones using the Project Finance for Permanence (PFP) approach.

## B

### Lack of mechanisms for site-specific monitoring and generation of data on climate, carbon, hydrology, ecosystem services, and land use impacts.
Both generation of and access to specific information on the impacts of climate change on ecosystems and human activities are critical for effective ecosystem-based adaptation (EbA) solutions — is still dispersed and in some instances out of reach for users at the local level. This lack of data and information limits the ability of decision-makers, communities, and other stakeholders to respond effectively to climate hazards.

### Limited capacity for the update and effective use of data to inform decision-making by SINAP, regional environmental authorities, municipal governments, and communities.
Currently, research institutes and universities are developing tools and platforms. However, it is necessary to generate capacities and mechanisms that make use of and articulate such information at the local and regional levels and guide more comprehensive analyses, decision making and action planning.

### Limited integration of national low-carbon, climate-resilient strategies into regional land use planning instruments due to lack of integrated institutional management and coordination.
Colombia has developed a number of tools for addressing climate change in its national development plans. However, the functioning of these tools is limited by their focus on specific sectors or areas, such as agriculture, energy, water resources, etc., and they are not yet fully integrated into instruments of public policy and planning, including those resulting from the peace agreement such as the Development Plans for Peace (PDPs). These plans are sectoral in nature and do not address land use issues comprehensively, limited particularly for protected areas. Therefore, empowering and increasing coordination of relevant authorities (e.g., ministries, regional environmental agencies, National Parks, municipalities, waterboards, etc.), based on a common vision and shared goals, is essential to ensure the integration of climate change into landscapes and increase management effectiveness, including maintaining and enhancing the delivery of critical ecosystem services.

### Failures in control over human threats to protected areas that diminish their capacity for carbon capture and storage, and water provision and regulation.
Lack, or limited articulation and collaboration between public authorities and local communities, is a major factor in these failures. These pressures from illegal actors, and some economic sectors — most remarkably agriculture and infrastructure—constitute the main threats to protected areas. In many cases, these pressures are seen as opposed to the interest of local families who partly depend on resources provided by the protected areas, or by economic sectors that seek to expand their intervention within the limits of these areas. This makes it necessary to strengthen the capacity of the protected areas to engage different stakeholders and resilient.

## Limited capacity of PA staff to exercise control and surveillance of the drivers of deforestation and unsustainable water exploitation.

### Project approach across mosaics

As described in further detail in Sections B.1 and 3, and the analysis in Annex 2 (and 2b), the mosaics and implementation areas are designed to address a balance of deforestation drivers, climate vulnerabilities, and opportunities for restoration and rehabilitation to improve ecosystem connectivity and maintain or enhance delivery of ecosystem services. The interventions within each mosaic target these drivers and vulnerabilities, with protected areas and ecosystems at their core. The interventions of each mosaic therefore represent a combination of landscape-scale approaches (e.g., governance initiatives, land-use planning), direct actions through restoration and rehabilitation, and on-farm interventions to improve adaptive capacity (see Table 5, Section B.1). For example, all mosaics are targeted for expropriation approaches, restoration and reclamation within initiatives, and on-farm adaptive capacity building through rainwater harvesting, vegetable gardens and other climate-smart agricultural practices.

These interventions vary slightly; however, depending on the relevant sector and based on local vulnerabilities. #### B.3. Project/programme description (max. 2500 words, approximately 5 pages)

**Project Overview**
- The project is a key part of Heritage Colombia (HECO), a broader, long-term umbrella program with a vision to protect and restore the most important areas in the next 20 years.
- It aims to reduce deforestation, forest degradation, land use changes, and other threats to the paramos, montane, lowland, and gallery forests within and adjacent to Protected Areas in the targeted geographies.

**Project Objectives**
1. Reduce deforestation, forest degradation, land use changes, and other threats.
2. Improve water quality and quantity by restoring ecosystems integrity and functionality.
3. Improve adaptive capacity for thousands of farmers increasing climate resilience and reducing vulnerability.
4. Increase direct adaptive capacity for farming households in and around protected areas to address these hazards.

**Project Activities**
- Implement ecosystem-based adaptation (EBA) and on-farm adaptation interventions across the project area.
- Support participatory monitoring systems to generate climate information used for improved decision-making in agriculture, forestry, and land management.
- Improve forest and land management and restoration rehabilitation to reduce carbon emissions and exposure of vulnerable communities to worsening climate hazards: drought and shifting water availability, landslides, and flooding.

**Expected Outcomes**
1. Increase adaptive capacity for farming households in and around protected areas by addressing these hazards through improved livelihoods and incomes.
2. Improve water storage and management systems, soil improvements, and farmer training schools.

**Ecosystem-based Adaptation (EBA) and On-Farm Adaptation Interventions**
- These interventions will be implemented across the project area to reduce vulnerability of local communities to climate change by reducing sensitivity and increasing adaptive capacity through improved land management practices.
- Climate-responsiveness in existing protected areas and adjacent lands (buffer zones and connectivity corridors), complemented by improved land management with farming communities, with the aim of reducing carbon emissions and exposure of vulnerable communities to worsening climate hazards: drought and shifting water availability, landslides, and flooding.

**Adaptation Services**
- These services support viable livestock production, for example, include soil regulation services underpinning stable plant production, micrometeorological work for wetter areas.

## Protection of Livestock and Water for Livestock and People

Therefore, climate impacts will also be addressed indirectly by targeting key drivers, like unsustainable productive practices, causing deforestation and thus loss of critical ecosystems, reducing resilience and increasing vulnerability to climate impacts, but also threatening the ecosystem services that underpin social-ecological resilience to climate change.

### The Expansion of the Protected Area Network

The expansion of the protected area network will target the protection of highly valuable moutainous habitats in the Andes. These areas are critical for maintaining water flow and providing water for downstream communities, reducing flooding and landslide risks, and sequestering carbon stocks essential to the country's long-term emissions reduction goals.

### Implementation of Ecosystem Restoration

Implementation of ecosystem restoration and rehabilitation within both protected areas and corridors will re-establish degraded ecosystems and improve resilience. In addition, 5,912 hectares will be rehabilitated over ten years in eight protected areas, through 101 implementation agreements, the training of 2,236 community members, and the provision of technical assistance.

### Improved Land and Forest Management Interventions

Improved land and forest management interventions will be implemented together with farming communities vulnerable to climate change. Shrubgrass, agroforestry, and agrosystematic solutions will help reduce these communities' sensitivity and improve their adaptive capacity to build climate resilient household productive systems. These interventions will improve productive systems for sustainable land use, reduce food insecurity and increase household income through the diversification of crops and livestock production.

### Training and Capacity Building

In addition, training will be provided to farmers to use these systems in response to increasing impacts

## B

### Colombia has two primary territorial environmental planning instruments: The Watershed and Marine Environmental Management Plan (POT, PBOT, EOT) and the instruments of environmental zoning (POMACA, PORH), in the context of the project.

#### 132. Colombia has two primary territorial environmental planning instruments: The Watershed and Marine Environmental Management Plan (POT, PBOT, EOT) and the instruments of environmental zoning (POMACA, PORH), in the context of the project.
- **The Watershed and Marine Environmental Management Plan (POT, PBOT, EOT):** This plan is developed through the coordinated use of natural resources (soil, water, flora and fauna) in a watershed is carried out. The population living in the basin participates in the development of the plan, which includes the identification of areas for conservation, sustainable use of renewable natural resources, the safe occupation of the territory, and avoiding activities that could cause environmental damage.
- **Instruments of Environmental Zoning (POMACA, PORH):** These instruments allow, through the relevant environmental authority, systematic intervention in water bodies to guarantee the quality and quantity of water. The POMACA is a territorial zoning instrument for the conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity, adaptation and mitigation of climate change, sustainable land development, green infrastructure, and ecosystem services.

#### 133. Environmental Determinants refer to laws and regulations that are hierarchically superior to Municipal Territorial Zoning Plans (POT, EOT and PBOT) and consist of all those norms, guidelines, and directives issued by the national and regional environmental authorities (MinAmbiente, Cau, PNIN). Therefore, municipal environmental planning must be in accordance with these laws and regulations. These instruments are applied to management, and forest protective reserves, among others. In turn, it is important to specifically integrate climate change considerations into territorial zoning plans at all levels of government, as well as to ensure that there is policy coherence at a local level.
- **Integrated Regional Climate Change Management Plans (PRICC):** These plans are developed by the national environmental authority and include various key stakeholders in its social component. Among these are the Presidential Council for Women, and the National Council for Sustainable Development (CND), among others.

#### 134. The Territorial Zoning Plan (POT) is the set of objectives, guidelines, policies, strategies, goals, actions and standards aimed at guiding and managing the physical development of the territory and the use of its resources in a sustainable manner. The territorial zoning plan must be developed according to the population of the municipality.
- **Territorial Zoning Plan (POT):** This plan applies to districts and municipalities with populations between 30,000 and 100,000 inhabitants.
- **Territorial Zoning Scheme (EOT):** This plan is applied in municipalities with a population of less than 30,000 inhabitants.

#### 135. In the Caribbean Coast, the activity will support the coordination of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta NP management plan with the territorial planning instruments of surrounding municipalities.
- **Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta NP Management Plan:** This plan is coordinated by the Fundación, POT, Fundación, PyVie, Algeciras, El Retén, Clenán, and Aracataca territorial planning instruments. In addition to this, WWF Colombia will implement an activity as EE.
- **Macarena - Chiribiquete Corridor:** WWF Colombia will implement this activity as EE.

#### 136. The following table lists the specific objectives of each activity under environmental management planning tools:
| Activity | Specific Objectives and Outputs |
|---------|--------------------------------|

### 1.8 Each for module and the corresponding selection/scenarios within them, technical information related to climate change impacts and adaptation measures will be incorporated into municipalities' territorial planning and watered management instruments.

In the first year of the project, key themes to be developed and the technical information related to climate change impacts and adaptation measures will be identified. The focus will be on short-term variability and hazards and longer-term shifts in water availability will be assessed. As of year two, annual reports will be generated for each landscape with a summary of the results of the analysis of the vulnerability of the management of the territory and the pertinent actions for their articulation will begin.

WWF Colombia will design and implement a training program for regional environmental authorities and municipalities in prioritized watersheds on the implementation of water resource planning instruments to address climate change impacts. The training will be done in two phases: one for 20 institutional actors and another for 80 community delegates from different landscapes, involving 46 people each.

### 1.10 Facilitate 4 annual intersectoral roundtables (i) cattle ranching, (ii) agriculture, (iii) water services, (iv) forest management, (v) private sector, (vi) indigenous peoples, (vii) women's organizations, (viii) local authorities, (ix) associations, community delegates and delegates from territorial institutions and national / presidential agencies (National Land Agency, Office of the Presidency Council for Stabilization and Consolidation) of land for the management of landscapes, involving 46 people each. ### Output 1.2 Community governance with SINAP and within connectivity corridors strengthened to improve climate-informed land and water use

#### 141. Strengthened governance by relevant actors within a landscape will lead to better management decisions for landscapes, as well as at the global level. It is recognized increasingly that when communities are properly trained, they have greater power to dialogue with other types of actors and ability to self-organize so that they can have a greater level of influence in political aspects and territorial management decisions. For this reason, training is included within this proposal such as the promotion of planning instruments of the communities (such as the plans, maps, and action plans) for the conservation of protected areas, the strengthening of dialogue with other actors in the territory and authorities, exchanges of experiences and the strengthening of intergenerational focus to improve dialogue and define targets to reduce deforestation and vulnerability to climate change.

#### 142. This output seeks to strengthen territorial community governance within landscapes to contribute to reducing pressures on ecosystems and to address the specific drivers of deforestation and priority climate hazards and longer-term risks such as desertification, soil erosion, water scarcity, biodiversity loss, forest fires, land degradation, drought, rainfall increasing seasonal variability, and flood risk. The strengthening of community governance includes activities that aim at improving the capacity for inclusive and co-responsible decision-making in landscapes, including greater participation in the decision-making bodies listed under the activities below and described in Annex 7, through support for internal decision-making spaces such as assemblies, meetings, workshops, exchanges, and through improved access to information.

#### 143. Eight climate governance schemes will be strengthened in the intervention landscapes: Caribbean Moscán; 1) Ciénaga Corridor; 2) Besós Perijá Corridor; 3) PNN Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta; Andes Mocana; 4) Coridor las Guajira; 5) Corredor del Chiribiquete; 6) Corredor del Magdalena Medio; 7) Chingaza Corridor; Amazon Moscán; 8) La Macarena-Chiribiquete Corridor; and 8) San Lucas Montañas.

Activity 1.2 Strengthen the capacity of local communities and their understanding of climate change, incorporating indigenous knowledge and gender responsiveness

This activity will promote education and training processes in community organizations and institutions in each landscape to improve their knowledge and capacities regarding the management of water resources and to provide them with the necessary tools for the implementation of strategies that contribute to addressing the drivers of deforestation and land use change and climate change, as well as to implement communications strategies in the four landscapes, based on the needs and priorities identified by the communities.

Training needs for community leaders and officials from local institutions who make decisions about territorial management on issues that contribute to addressing the drivers of deforestation and land use change and climate change will be provided. This training will include strengthening the capacity of indigenous women's leaders of the areas, of educational centers in environmental education, and of communication strategies for the general population regarding the conservation, appreciation, and awareness of the identified climate problem, which will improve management decisions in the landscapes.

On the other hand, the knowledge and traditional practices of use and management of nature by indigenous peoples. Alto-descendents, and local communities have made possible the conservation of ecosystem services in the landscapes. However, this knowledge is being lost due to factors such as the weakening of the traditional structures that transmit it from one generation to another, the migration and loss of interest by younger generations, and the loss of sacred places, among others.

The focus of this activity is to promote and recover traditional knowledge and practices that contribute to climate change mitigation and adaptation. This will be done through a series of workshops with indigenous leaders identified with the indigenous organizations of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, the Community Councils of Candelaria, the DM San Agustín-Chirijito, the DM La Guajira, the DM Tumaco, the DM Chingaza, and the DM Arari-Guayabalé communities. This activity will also promote the strengthening and training of women's leaders in the management of natural resources, as well as the implementation of a strategy for the conservation of sacred places, landraces, and flooding risks.

In the Amazon Mosaic, within the framework of the Inter-institutional Committee for Environmental Education (CIEE), it will be implemented through the activities of the Amazon Vision Program and GEF Heart of the Amazon. The activity will strengthen environmental education in schools and communities by strengthening the capacities of the School Environmental Projects-PreSE on water resources and climate change, as well as the capacity building of the Community Action Boards of San Jose del Guaviare and El Retorno. The activity will strengthen environmental education in schools and communities through the implementation of a strategy for communications focused on both the deforestation drivers of climate change, land use change, and new extremes, including extreme rains, heat, variability, drought, and floods. This strategy seeks to promote knowledge and awareness among community leaders and officials from local institutions of the municipalities of Guaviare and El Retorno concerning management of water resources and forest ecosystems.

In the Orinoco Transition Mosaic, the environmental education and communications strategy of the PIN Chingaza will be implemented in the communities of San Juanito, El Calvario, Fomeque, Choique y La Caleta. The activity will strengthen the capacity building of community leaders and officials from local institutions such as Fundación como Asociación de la Comunidad Indígena del Municipio de Chingaza, Fundación Conserva y Asocietra will also be strengthened under a gender and indigenous peoples' approach.

Finally, in the Caribbean Mosaic, the communication and environmental education strategy of the PIN SNSM management plan will be implemented. This strategy will include support for the San Lorenzo Experimental Station as an environmental education center managed jointly between the PMN and the four indigenous peoples in the mosaic.

## Activity 1.1.7: Shift access and revenue generation of royalties (regalias) to climate responsive planning and development within the project landscapes

### B

181. To ensure the financial sustainability of project outcomes in protected areas and surrounding landscapes there is a need to shift the destination of government funds and resources to climate-responsive planning and development within the project landscapes.
182. This will be achieved by:
- 11.6: Providing technical assistance to the Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Parks (MENRyP) and Colombia’s Public Corporations (CPs), to relevant funding sources. To this end, eleven (11) financial mechanisms (Environmental Investment Trust Fund (EITF), National Forest Fund (NFF), National Biodiversity Fund (NBIF), National Water Fund (NWf), Compulsory contribution of 1% (Article 111), Water use rate, imposition of collecting property tax in Protected Areas, and others) were analyzed. The eleven mechanisms were evaluated based on their potential to generate resources for priority action that took into account legal and institutional elements, ease of implementation and scalability.
- 183: Financial instruments were selected from a range of national instruments with potential to contribute to the project objectives.

### General System of Royalties (SGR)

184. The General System of Royalties (SGR) mechanism received highest scores among the analyzed mechanisms in terms of its capacity to generate resources for priority actions that took into account legal and institutional elements, ease of implementation and scalability.
185. These resources for environmental and climate purposes by different project stakeholders, their potential for scalability and replicability across four landscapes and the fact that resources would not be diverted for other purposes, such as debt service.

### The SGR in Colombia

186. The SGR was established in 1991, but has been recently modified by two legal reforms (Law 1530 of 2012 and Law 2056 of 2020) to decentralize and distribute the resources obtained through the exploitation of non-renewable natural resources. The SGR is a mechanism that allows for the generation of resources from the extraction of natural resources, which are then used to finance environmental and sustainable development investment projects.
187. The different categories of investment projects to be financed by the SGR include: (i) projects related to the conservation and restoration of ecosystems; (ii) projects focused on environmental issues, and local environmental priorities. Since the 2020 reform of royalty allocation, the SGR is now managed by the National System for Strategic Environmental Areas (SNAE), which is in the formulation process.
188. Furthermore, while the government of Colombia enacted a new decree (No. 3457 of COVID-19) to establish that SGR resources will be allocated according to the National Strategy for Strategic Environmental Areas, which is in the formulation process.

### In order to enhance access to this funding

189. In order to enhance access to this funding, there is a need for a broad institutional framework at central, regional and local levels that requires territorial entities to interact with each other and have strong capacity in the design of projects and proposals.
190. The SGR mechanism will be used as an instrument to provide resources to the MENRyP and CPs to build their capacities to formulate projects and to review calls for proposals considering the allocations of the SGR. Capacity building programs will be designed with a focus on strengthening the capacity of territorial entities, which would allow for the creation of alliances with a broader scope and enable the different eligible entities to access funding allocated by them.

### According to the projections

191. According to the projections and due to the location of large extractive companies in the Caribbean region, this is the largest potential for mobilization of royalty payments for environmental investment projects in this region.
192. Therefore, the capacity building strategy for structuring environmental investment projects will begin with this landscape and will be extended to other landscapes where there are large extractive companies that could generate resources to further enable scaling and replication in other municipalities, departments and environmental authorities in Colombia.

### The project aims

193. The project aims to increase the overall number of projects presented and approved under the environmental allocations of the SGR.
194. This will be achieved by strengthening the capacity of territorial entities to design proposals that address climate change and drivers of deforestation.
195. By creating guidelines and capacity building programs, that may be developed in collaboration with other actors such as universities, research centers, civil society organizations, climate-resilient measures, and improvement of livelihoods, this activity supports national planning instruments and regulations that establish royalties as the public financial instrument for supporting the national development plan.

**Component 3: LAND MANAGEMENT IMPROVED AND RESTORATION IMPLEMENTED TO REDUCE CARBON EMISSIONS AND STRENGTHEN ADAPTIVE CAPACITY OF VULNERABLE COMMUNITIES**

Output 3.1 Management of protected areas improved to reduce deforestation and maintain or enhance ecosystem integrity and functionality for climate change.

The National Forest System (SINAP) covers an area of SINAP (after the Spanish name) covers 31,578,968 hectares (10% of the Nation's territory), which includes community owned, private, and public protected areas, local, regional, and national areas. As discussed in Section B.1., the protected areas within SINAP conserve vast stocks of carbon and also provide ecosystem services such as water provisioning for urban populations in Colombia. Providing drinking water for more than 25 million people in the country is one of the main functions provided by the forest ecosystems managed under SINAP. The area provides other provisioning services for urban populations in Colombia, providing drinking water for more than 25 million people in the country is one of the main functions provided by the forest ecosystems managed under SINAP. The area also provides current geographical and ecological coverage of the SINAP, the proportion of the natural and cultural patrimony it protects and the number of species that are protected.

Output 3.2 Management of private reserves improved to reduce deforestation and maintain or enhance ecosystem integrity and functionality for climate change.

In addition to the National Parks managed by PINN, National Protective Forest Reserves and National Integrated Management Districts are also part of the national system. Although they are formally under the jurisdiction of the Autonomous Regions (CARs), Regional protected areas (e.g., Regional Park, Regional Integrated Management District) are also included in SINAP. These areas include the 107 private reserves managed by PINN and the 245 CARS. Finally, there are a large number of private reserves within SINAP in Colombia, especially in the Andes. These reserves are located on land that is not part of any public or protected area and are managed as private property for an ecosystem and is voluntarily managed by the owner for purposes of conservation and sustainable use. These reserves are mainly in areas that can protect important ecological features such as endemic species, watersheds, etc.

Output 3.3 Management of indigenous territories improved to reduce deforestation and maintain or enhance ecosystem integrity and functionality for climate change.

## 3.1.2 Expansion of Sierra Nevada Santa Marta National Park by an additional 181,753 hectares to reduce deforestation threats, preserve forest connectivity, and protect source waters.
The proposed expansion of the Sierra Nevada Santa Marta National Park by approximately 181,753 hectares will increase representation in the dry tropical zone of SINAP and protect headwaters and hydrological services that contribute to agricultural production downstream. There is as yet no definitive proposal of the expansion, but it is expected to be based on long-duration dialogues, including the evaluation of alternative management regimes, and the Specific Agreements signed by the indigenous peoples and communities in the area will serve as a basis for the declaration of the expansion, including the "Joint Management Plan" between indigenous groups and SINAP.

## 3.1.2 Monitoring and evaluation of designation process, including safeguards monitoring.
This activity will take place in the southern sector of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta National Park (Park), which is located on the Caribbean coast of Colombia, in the department of Magdalena, in the region of the Caribbean, in jurisdictions of the municipalities of Ciénaga, San Juan del Cesar, Fundación, Aracataca, Dibulla, Mutis, Mompox, Riohacha, Puerto Bello, and Quibdo.

The initiative to expand the Sierra Nevada Santa Marta National Park was successfully acceded in the mountain massif of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta (SNSM), which is the first territory that has been requested by the Arhuaco and Kogui Indigenous Peoples for the protection of the ancestral territory delimited by the "Black Line" which refers to the original extent of their territories. The expansion will also include areas where the traditional lands of the Wayuú, Emberá, and Miskito peoples are represented in the current SINAP. It also provides recognition of the traditional management by the indigenous peoples of the ancestral territory of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta National Park, as well as the implementation of the route for the declaration of new protected areas (according to Resolution 1215 of 2015 of the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development). The expansion will also include the territories of the Malayo-Arhuaco Resguardo, the Resguardo Arhuaco de La Sierra, PNN, the Alliance for the Conservation of Nature and Culture (ACNOC), Fundación Colombia, Fundación Mario Sandoval y Fundación Grupo Aves, WCS, WWF, and the Natural Wealth Program.

The declaration process began with the Kogui and Arhuaco indigenous peoples' characterization and identification of sacred sites and priority areas for conservation and ancestral management in the proposed territories.

### 214. The expansion of the protected area is aimed at strengthening the protection of strategic ecosystems critical for carbon sequestration, ecosystem services provision (including biodiversity), and cultural diversity.

Under the framework of the SNSMIP, the areas are managed by the indigenous peoples who have a direct relationship with these territories and their resources. The management of the protected areas is overseen by a joint committee of PNN and Indigenous authorities, also ensuring any other relevant actors are involved in decision-making processes. It should be noted that the survival of the Peoples is completely linked to the territory they inhabit and the two-way relationship between territory and being indigenous.

### 215. The SNSMIP mission is strategic for the Caribbean Caribbean, since there are about 18 main rivers that supply water to the region (e.g., Magdalena, Cesar, and La Guajira). It plays a key role as a climate regulator of the subregion, with influence on the entire Caribbean region. It establishes a clear relationship of water connectivity with other protected areas in Colombia such as the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta National Park, Tayrona and Salamanca Island National Parks and the Los Flamencos Fauna Sanctuary (PRNC 2015). Climate change is expected to have significant impacts on these ecosystems through changes in temperature, precipitation-related physicochemical processes, and therefore ecosystem dynamics. These impacts and resultant ecological changes will affect the water cycle, including changes in river flow and biodiversity associated with bodies of water; decrease in water quality, decrease in ice coverage in glaciers, increase in flooding probability to fire, effects on crops and diseases, and changes in the patterns of distribution and abundance of many species.

### 216. The main objective will be to strengthen the capacity of communities in the management of protected areas by enabling the communities to lead to a more coordinated exercise of control of natural resources in protected areas and corridors with greater confidence than the actors and with a focus on action to control deforestation and the determination of the types of pressures that affect them. ##### 232. One of the control and surveillance tools this suite will support is SMART (Spatial Monitoring and Reporting Tool). SMART is a mobile application for field management tool designed to assist rangers on the ground to do their job more effectively and efficiently. It has been implemented in more than 600 PA across the world and it is currently being used by over 1,500 users in 28 countries. SMART uses GPS-enabled smartphones or other mobile devices. SMART streamlines collection and analysis of data on important environmental indicators, such as biodiversity, forest cover, land use change, and human activity. It also provides real-time alerts for suspicious activities and the detection of subtle changes and responses in environments undergoing change due to climate change and climate variability. SMART can help in the allocation of scarce resources for effective protection by identifying hot-spots or implementing complementary and coordinated communication among rangers, community patrols, park managers, and system administrators.

#### Rehabilitation interventions for the mosaics are described below:

- In the case of the Caribbean Conservation Mosaic in the Sierra Marta NP-Cenago Grande Corridor implementation site, the activity will support the establishment of agroforestry systems and living fencelines in coffee and cocoa plantations to enable sustainable production that is also resilient against climate change. The project will use synthetic bee stakes in orchards to increase pollination variability.
- In the PPN SNSM Corridor implementation site - PNRS Bcesos -, PNJR Bcesos -. PNJR Rio Seco basin and Guacuabo Corridor, the activity will support the establishment of agroforestry systems and living fencelines in coffee plantations in the middle basin of the Cesar River, involving agroforestry systems of coffee, cocoa, fruit trees, and living fences with cattle plantations, as well as plans for sustainable and resilient production in the Guacuabo and Guacamayo sectors.
- In the PPN SNMS Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta Corridor - PNRS Bcesos -, PNJR Serranía del Perijá implementation site, the activity will support establishment of agroforestry systems and other agrosystems, together with the use of synthetic bee stakes in coffee plantations to increase pollination variability. The project will also promote sustainable use that conserves strategic ecosystems and it in turn produces economic benefits to communities, contributing to the conservation of biodiversity.
- For the Orinooco Transition Conservation Mosaic at the San Juan-Erlo Calaparío implementation site in the Guaytuba river basin, efforts will focus on the design and implementation of a participatory agricultural planning program for 100 producer families living within the buffer zone of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta National Park, mainly with bean and cattle producers. Management alternatives will seek to address deforestation and degradation of natural resources in the area by promoting sustainable use of forest resources through the use of synthetic bee stakes in orchards. Project participants will work with 100 producer families under conservation agreements, which provide Incentives for the proper planning in return for a producer leaving an area for conservation.

##### The long-term financial sustainability of landscape management as envisioned in this proposal will depend on investments by the private sector in nature-based solutions to climate change. In the face of the economic and social crisis caused by the coronavirus pandemic there is an especially urgent need to support the transition to a green, fair, inclusive economy that creates jobs, reduces poverty and other forms of exclusion, revitalizes communities, creates jobs, addresses inequality, and drives inclusive growth.

##### The challenges to private sector investment include mobilizing funds at the scale needed and identifying a business case for nature-based solutions. To address these challenges by augmenting information on three nature-based sectors, identifying growth opportunities for businesses within these sectors, and providing technical assistance to help them develop their business cases and other forms of support, such as seed level enterprises and SMIs in production systems and value chains for agroforestry, coffee, cacao, tropical fruits, and ecotourism and public, private and blended investment facilities.
