### G.1 Environmental and Social Assessment (max. 750 words, approximately 1.5 pages)

**538. The project will comply with GCF’s Environmental and Social Policy (ESP), including the Policy on the Prevention and Protection from Sexual Exploitation, Sexual Abuse, and Sexual Harassment (SEAH) and Indigenous Peoples Policy (IPP) through application of WWF's Environmental and Social Safeguards Framework (ESAF). The project will also comply with GCF’s Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI) policy on GBV & SEAH. The project has been screened as Category “B” given that it is essentially a climate change mitigation project, which may have adverse environmental impacts but no significant social or economic risks and environmental benefits. Any adverse environmental and social impacts are site specific and can be mitigated through the implementation of appropriate measures at the operational level to ensure any activities that move forward have a low or medium level of risk before proceeding.**

**525. An Environmental and Social Management Framework (ESMF) (Annex 6), including an Indigenous Peoples Planning Framework (IPPF) and a Process Framework (PF), has been prepared to define project-level environmental and social management processes, as well as the roles and responsibilities for each process. Additionally, in-depth analysis of the security and conflict situation has been completed as part of the ESMF risk mitigation plan as a separate Security Assessment (Appendix 3 of the ESMF) and a Safety and Security Protocol (Appendix 4 of the ESP).**

**528. The project is required to comply with WWF’s Standard on Environment and Social Risk Management, the Standard on Grievance Mechanisms, the Standard on Stakeholder Engagement, and the Guidance Note on Gender-based Violence (GBV) and Sexual Exploitation, Abuse and Harassment (SEAH).**

**527. The proposed formulation process has involved consultations with different types of stakeholders (communities, local governments, public entities, NGOs) at different levels (national, regional and local) using a gender-sensitive approach that ensures the participation of women and men. During the 2020-2021 period, around 260 meetings and workshops were held involving around 1,242 people from which feedback was received. (See Annex 7 Stakeholder Engagement Plan, SEP).**

**528. In addition to the aforementioned standards which are applicable to all WWF GCF AE projects, this project has triggered the following standards:**

**529. Overall, activities of the project will produce significant conservation and climate mitigation and adaptation benefits and any potential adverse environmental impacts on human populations or important natural habitats will be avoided or minimized through the implementation of appropriate measures that directly targets protecting and restoring natural habitats; strengthening local communities’ ability to conserve their natural resources; supporting sustainable transforming markets and policies to reduce the impact of the production and consumption of commodities.**

#### Standard on Restriction of Access and Resettlement

**530. There will be no land acquisition or involuntary resettlement of individuals and/or families under the project. The project includes activities to ensure that local communities are involved in the management of the NPA’s through land use and management agreements, and to establish community water associations. These activities may restrict or prohibit the extraction of resources in certain areas of the NPAs and corridors, thereby restricting access to

## Standard on Indigenous Peoples

This standard is triggered because there are indigenous and Afro-descendant communities living in the Caribbean and San Lucas **1** mosaics, in all other mosaics they are only the presence of possible ancestral communities. The main indigenous peoples in the Caribbean mosaic are the Kogui, Kankuamo, and the Arhuaco. Afro-Colombian communities include those in Guachoque and Guacochito municipalities within the department of Magdalena, as well as the Afro-descendant communities surrounding the city of Valledupar in the department of Cesar, and the community council of Obatalá located in the municipality of Fundación within the department of Magdalena. As the specific activities and locations of these communities are not known with certainty, they have been included in this proposal as part of the ESF.

In the meeting held with the Indigenous Organizations of the Caribbean landscape, a 3-month interaction process was achieved with the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta indigenous organizations. During the interaction process, general information was provided regarding the project and the spaces created for interaction were used to discuss the project in detail. The participants agreed on the creation of the logical framework and the specific activities that will be carried out, that are of interest to the indigenous peoples. The organizations also made specific recommendations about social and cultural safeguards.

The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta and San Lucas mosaics present a very low level of conservation coverage in their territories. Therefore, the declaration of conservation areas and the organization process is in a preliminary stage based on the legal roadmap for the creation of a possible new protected area. The preliminary stages are fulfilled with the logic framework and the specific activities that will be carried out during project implementation.

The AE has not been formally undertaken but will proceed along with project implementation. However, the AE has assessed the potential impacts of the project in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta mosaic. In the case of the Caribbean mosaic, it does not involve changes in land use, and the likely impact it will have on indigenous peoples is related to the creation of a conservation area that could enhance the protection of land rights of the indigenous peoples and other communities in the area.

In parallel to the creation of the conservation area, a resguardo huanca has also very recently been created in the area. That process is also being led by the national government and has an impact on indigenous territories. The AE will be carried out once the resguardo huanca is officially declared by the government. If the proposed protected area will overlap with any indigenous group's territory, a prior and informed consent process must be followed in accordance with Colombian law. The declaration of any type of protected area will include agreements with all communities and institutions in the area. Consultation processes are also being carried out to promote land tenure security for indigenous peoples, to promote rights of landless communities and define restoration, conservation and well-being investments that could enhance the protection of land rights.

During the consultation and participation process with indigenous organizations, the organization were directly consulted, in accordance with national legislation and WWF requirements that requires processes of consultation and free, prior and informed consent of any initiative or project. For this reason, the indigenous organizations of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta were specifically summoned and participated.

## Gender assessment and action plan (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)

- The mainstreaming of gender perspectives is understood as a dual process in which an analysis is carried out on the way in which gender relations affect the intentions proposed for the project as well as the ways in which the project will impact existing gender relations and opportunities to address these relations between men and women from different communities. This is in order to make visible opportunities to address inequalities and promote equality, and to ensure that the project does not exacerbate or reinforce existing inequalities.
- The project's gender analysis was developed through combining different information-gathering methods including desk reviews of relevant literature, interviews with key informants, and official sources and project documents. The main content was shaped by guiding questions developed following a review of the literature on gender in the context of climate change adaptation.
- Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, it was not possible to hold face-to-face meetings with local actors to directly collect contextual information about gender relations and opportunities for addressing inequalities. Instead, the project organized virtual meetings/workshops in which exchanges with various regional/local and national action providers accessed to primary sources of information, including inquiries among these actors which included women leaders and

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V3.0 | PAGE 183

## Gender assessment and action plan (Annex G)

The gender assessment (Annex G) provides detailed socio-demographic information on the country and the project interaction areas, regarding the situation of both urban and rural women, their access to resources, decision-making roles, relationships with men, and their exposure to different forms of the continuum of gender-based violence and SEAH. It gives a perspective of the scenario in which the project will operate and provides an understanding of the structural inequalities that exist within the country to improve their condition generally and as it relates to their increased vulnerability to climate change. The results of this assessment are used to develop a gender action plan, which is part of the overall detailed gender action plan. The following is a summary of important results obtained from the gender assessment:

- **Structural gender inequalities** are a historical legacy in Colombia, and it is reflected in the unequal distribution of power, capital, lack of access to financing, work, and livelihoods.
- These inequalities are particularly pronounced among rural women, women with disabilities, indigenous women, Afro-Colombian women, urban women, ethnic belonging, etc.).
- In Colombia, there is a strong interplay between structural gender mechanisms and the institutions in charge of environmental issues. The strongest articulation occurs at the level of social organizations.
- Although there are very significant advances in access to education for women, gender gaps in terms of age, ethnicity, and rural/urban residence persist. Women continue to bear the burden of care work, which particularly heavily on rural women, even more so on women from ethnic minorities.
- There is a strong interplay between structural gender inequalities and climate change, especially for rural women, as well as national and international commitments for their promotion. However, it appears that these commitments have yet to reverse inequality and temporarily benefit a small number of women.

Based on the above, the project aims to mainstream gender throughout each project component by strengthening the capacity of all actors involved in the project to recognize, understand, change, adapt, and gender dimensions, while promoting the linking, strengthening, leadership and empowerment of groups of women and men. The project will also seek to address structural inequalities that are at the root of current and potential gender inequalities. The project also aims to make visible the contributions that women make in environmental management and climate change adaptation and mitigation.

### Gender Action Plan (Annex G)

The Gender Action Plan (Annex G) provides detailed gender-specific actions, associated indicators and targets. The project aims to be gender-responsive through its activities, outputs and outcomes that reflect a gender perspective. The plan is based on the results of the gender assessment and identifies how it engages women and men to provide equal opportunities and distribution of benefits. It highlights the role of the project gender specialist within the PMU, who is responsible for supervising gender/sexual inclusion strategies and ensuring their implementation throughout all stages of the project. The plan also provides a project staff and stakeholders as needed on gender throughout the life of the project. The following provides a list of key actions that will be taken to mainstream gender in each component of the project and the gender action plan:

- Develop gender-sensitive indicators and targets for all activities, outputs, and outcomes at all levels of women and men.
- Develop gender-sensitive strategies and plans for all activities, outputs, and outcomes with gender dimensions in environmental management, protected areas and climate policy and actions.
- Develop gender-sensitive strategies and plans for the inclusion of a gender approach in all aspects of Protected Areas Management as part of a specific gender strategy.
- Ensure authorities, technical experts and representatives of government and civil society institutions recognize women’s contributions to the conservation of wetlands and forests and other ecosystems and support their empowerment and agency.
- Ensure that climate change adaptation and mitigation strategies and measures do no harm and take gender dimensions into account.

# G.3. Financial management and procurement (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)

## 546. WWF grants management and subrecipient monitoring is supported by a grants management system that includes a project tracking module. This module provides notifications for due dates of deliveries (from the grant recipient to and from the donor), tracks disbursements, and monitors progress against budget settings (if applicable) and identifies risks so that project supervision as a whole is informed and documented.

## 547. During project implementation, WWF will provide oversight and quality assurance in accordance with the terms of the GCF grant agreement and any other relevant agreements (e.g., subrecipient agreement (in the form of a grant agreement)). This may include, but is not limited to, monitoring spot checks, facilitation, and participation in project steering committee meetings, quarterly progress and annual performance reports, and other reporting as required by the GCF.

## 548. WWF will advance funds to FPN and WWF Colombia (for the implementation of agreed and approved project activities), through quarterly disbursements based on spending projections included with each project budget. The actual expenditures for each quarter will be reported to the GCF within 30 days after the end of that quarter, and any remaining balance in the project’s budget will be returned to the GCF. Project expenses will be reported semi-annually to the GCF (at the mid-year financial report and the Annual Financial Report). Any interest earned on funds received from WWF Colombia or FPN Patrimonio Natural will receive these disbursements, and any interest accrued during the project will be refunded to the GCF, as well as any amount of investment income paid by WWF Colombia or FPN Patrimonio Natural to the GCF Proceeds, as well as the amount of such Investment Income paid to the GCF for each calendar year of the project will be submitted annually by March 30 along with an unaudited financial statement per WWF’s audit.

## 549. All projects are audited annually following the WWF project audit guidelines. The project will have two annual audits: (1) WWF engages Grant Thornton (an internationally recognized audit firm, who was selected by WWF Colombia and FPN Patrimonio Natural) to perform an annual audit of the EEs’ accounts per GCF requirements; and (2) WWF will require that both EEs (WWF Colombia and Fundo Patrimônio Natural) engage an independent auditor to perform a separate annual audit in accordance with the GCF’s requirements as defined by GCF. A scheduled audit is used to determine whether the funds transferred to the Executing Entities were used for the purposes intended, and whether the EEs are in compliance with the GCF’s rules, including the EE’s assessed policies and procedures. The annual project audit based on the calendar year, will be submitted to the GCF by June 30, for each year of execution.

## 550. For FPN Colombia, WWF Colombia submits work plans, budget annual procurement plans to the AE. FWN and WWF Colombia submit requests for disbursements. Reporting from all co-EEs will be consolidated by the PMU and submitted to the AE. WWF will then submit Annual Performance Reports (APRs) and Financial Statements (FS) as required.

## 551. Both Fundo Patrimonio and WWF Colombia have procurement policies that meet the WWF AE minimum standards. Procurement will be executed according to the approved annual procurement plan and the EEs’ procurement policy.

## 552. This project will follow WWF’s financial reporting templates and formats which are in line with internationally recognized reporting standards, as well as the GCF’s required reporting templates.

# Secretariat’s assessment of FP203

## Proposal name: Heritage Colombia (HECO): Maximizing the Contributions of Sustainably Managed Landscapes in Colombia for Achievement of Climate Goals

### Accredited entity: World Wildlife Fund, Inc. (WWF)

### Country/ies: Colombia

### Project/programme size: Medium

## I. Overall assessment of the Secretariat

1. The funding proposal is presented to the Board for consideration with the following remarks:

| Strengths | Points of caution |
| --- | --- |
| The proposal has a very solid financial exit strategy, having secured in excess of the necessary funds required for implementation through two public financial instruments: repurchase agreements and a 20-year resolution 50%, issued in May 2012, entities in property to absorb up to 17.3% of carbon revenues for the project. | While the proposal effectively addresses the drivers of deforestation and ecosystem degradation in Colombia’s natural areas and buffer areas, it does not address the broader drivers of deforestation and ecosystem degradation at national level. To mitigate this risk, the proposal (i) should address deforestation drivers at the national level; and (ii) should include a mechanism for conservation to counter the sustained pressure for deforestation coming from drivers beyond the landscapes. |
| The proposal is very efficient, with a cost of €20/0.5 tCO2 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent of GCF investment over the project lifetime and a cost of €13/0.5 tCO2 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent of indirect beneficiary. |  |
| The project will also deliver co-benefits, including biodiversity and clean water provision and regulation. |

The proposal relies on conservation, restoration and rehabilitation interventions that have been tried and tested in a wide range of ecosystems and social settings. The accredited entity has strong capacity to replicate these activities across the world in implementing these activities and producing results in terms of climate change mitigation and adaptation.

2. The Board may wish to consider approving this funding proposal with the terms and conditions set out in annexure A, short term addendum IX titled “List of proposed conditions and recommendations.”

## Summary of the Secretariat’s assessment

### Project background

1. The proposed project is a cornerstone of the WWF strategy for the conservation of Colombia's varied ecosystems. It falls under the Heritage Colombia (HECO) Programme, a public-private partnership designed to secure financing and long-term sustainability for large-scale landscape management initiatives.
2. The project will be implemented by Bluefields International in collaboration with private philanthropic funding and uniting them around a common goal that combines conservation and sustainable development.

### The goal of the project

1. The goal of the project is to shift to a new paradigm of sustainable landscape finance which brings together (i) climate-resilient management of areas in and around protected areas, (ii) support for local communities, and (iii) innovative financing mechanisms that enhance resilience of local livelihoods.

### Project sites

1. The proposed project features the following in this proposal over 6.4 million hectares or 5.8 per cent of the country's territory, amounting to a third of the HECO goal of conserving 20 million hectares at national level.
   - These mosaics are: Caribbean, San Lucas, the Central Andes, Orito Valley, and the Eastern Plains.
2. The project sites were selected for their potential for maximizing biodiversity conservation in Colombia's ecosystems and climate challenges.

### Building on an approved GCF project

1. Building on an approved GCF project, FP50: Biodiva for Life, this project will address long-standing financing gaps for conservation by blending funding from donors and increasing government contributions.
2. The project, which is a 30-year commitment with a 10-year implementation period and co-finance, will exceed baselines by an additional USD 102 million to finance the transition to the sustainable landscape model.
3. In addition to the USD 548 million in GCF funding, the project will secure new public domestic resources, notably through royalties and a carbon tax - see annex for details of these contributions.
4. Over this period, the project will therefore leverage a total of USD 207 million, or close to five times the GCF investment.

### Project benefits

1. The project will benefit 229,658 people directly by enhancing capacity to use climate information and manage climate risks on farms, as well through the restored and rehabilitated ecosystems.
2. Indirectly, it will benefit an additional 30 million people in Colombia who rely on water from protected areas for their livelihoods.

### The total mitigation impact

1. The total mitigation impact from reduced deforestation, forest restoration and preserved sinks is 8.9 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (MTCO2e) at project completion.
2. This translates to a GCF contribution of USD 305 million or approximately 46 per cent of USD 0.92 per tCO2e for GCF finance.
3. This project would contribute between 13.8 and 17.8 per cent of the targeted reduction of greenhouse gases (GHGs) in Colombia's nationally determined contribution (NDC).

## 3.2 Paradigm shift potential

Scale: Medium to high

The core paradigm shift potential of this proposal centers on the financial exit strategy based on the WWF approach. The HEO PFF approach builds on a similar GCF project, FPGB (Financing for Life), which has been implemented in Colombia and other countries that use the PFF approach—Amazon Region Protected Areas, Forever Costa Rica, and the Great Bear Rainforest Project. These projects have demonstrated that it is possible to generate revenue from donor funds and more than USD 600 million in in-country financial commitments to preserve natural resources.

In this project, the implementation of the PFF approach involves using upfront funds, including GCF finance, during a transition period to create the conditions to secure a long-term flow of carbon revenues. At the end of the transition period and throughout the remaining life of the project life, ongoing recurring costs are estimated at USD 7.2 million per year, which will be covered by the carbon revenue stream (approximately USD 10-15 million annually or USD 93 million). Over the 10 years of the project implementation period, GCF funds will attract an additional USD 486 million in private sector investment and USD 72.5 million from other sources. The project will leverage an additional USD 206 million—close to five times the GCF investment.

The revenue expected from the carbon tax was further bolstered by Government Resolution No. 139, issued in May 2022, which increases the rate of carbon tax revenue for HEOS itself.

The potential for project replicability and scalability is very also strong. All three national parks have access to landscape information that can be immediately scaled to the entirety of Colombia’s protected area system through critical monitoring, and the learning from this project will be used to scale up the approach in other landscapes. Knowledge-sharing and increasing capacities to use and apply climate-relevant information are key factors for replicability. The project will also develop a suite of tools and monitoring systems and targeted activities to generate inter-institutional knowledge management processes built on landscape-specific documentation and knowledge gathering.

## 3.3 Sustainable development potential

Scale: High

As a project focused primarily on ecosystems and especially forests, the proposal’s co-benefits are numerous and centred on ecosystem services, including biodiversity and the provision of carbon sequestration.


---

disturbance. Forest protected areas are known to be effective, and can have 14.5 per cent more trees than similar ecosystems outside protected areas. In addition, forest restoration in biodiversity-unfriendly degraded landscapes enhances biodiversity persistence and the delivery of ecosystem services.

The Amazon in particular hosts an extraordinary range of species, which has earned Colombia the status of "megadiverse country". Biodiversity offers a wide range of benefits such as medical research (e.g., the discovery of the drug artemisinin from the sweet wormwood), the de-lance snake venom, helps hundreds of millions of people around the world control hypertension.

### Water provision and regulating services. In addition to biodiversity, protected areas preserve many ecosystem services such as the provision of water and the regulation of water flow. These services are estimated at US$ 10 billion annually in Colombia. The project will support management of modified ecosystems such as agricultural landscapes. Research shows that 50 per cent of the total value of Colombian agriculture is derived from these areas, with an annual market value of USD 582 million annually. Drinking water for 25 million people is provided by 19 protected areas for a value of USD 491 million annually.

### A third reason for the project is to support Colombia in the provision of ecosystem services crucial to a population with a majority (52.6 per cent) living below the poverty line. This proposal offers the opportunity to address this issue by supporting the conservation and restoration of natural protected areas, hence the request for grants in the context of this project.

Thirdly, 78 per cent of the population in the selected areas live below the poverty line. The conflict with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) has left over from the conflict period. Recovery of communities from the dislocations left over from the conflict period and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) is a priority for the Colombian government, which considers it appropriate for a more equitable wealth distribution that requires stricter controls on the management of protected areas and immediately surrounding that favour both conservation and local livelihoods.

In terms of gender, 35.7 per cent of women and 28.7 per cent of men over 15 years of age in rural households are illiterate. Women-headed rural households suffer from exterior monetary deprivation, which severely limits adaptive capacity to climate change. The lack of access to information on weather monitoring and production is therefore a key need addressed in the design of this proposal.

**Ecosystems and Biodiversity Conservation**

The project will not fund activities that will purposefully introduce non-native species, including genetically modified organisms (GMOs) and invasive species. The project (Component II) also excludes forest ecosystem restoration activities, unless they are part of a larger ecological intervention such as reforestation, terraces, or other non-natural interventions. Thus, while the project may support some aspects of forest ecosystem restoration, it will not fund projects that focus solely on this activity.

The project is expected to be consistent with national policies and strategies for the adoption and implementation of forest ecosystem restoration activities/technologies. Any measure that involves reforestation or afforestation should be based on scientific studies and documented successes locally or with similar ecological features elsewhere.

### GCF Indigenous Peoples Policy and ESSE 7: Indigenous peoples

The project will involve indigenous peoples and Afro-descendant communities. Project activities provide the potential for co-benefits in strengthening participation of indigenous peoples and communities in climate change adaptation planning and decision-making, as well as in sustainable resource management and indigenous knowledge. To safeguard rights of affected indigenous peoples and communities under national law, an Indigenous Peoples' Planning Framework (IPPF) has been prepared to clarify the principles, structures and organizational arrangements that will be applied. The IPPF provides policy and procedures to screen project impacts on indigenous peoples and communities. In addition, a Gender Action Plan (GAP) is being developed. Community organizations may be included as sub-grantees in the project. Recognizing the potential for conflict between project activities and existing land uses, a Conflict Sensitivity Analysis will be conducted. Within the Gender Assessment and Action Plan, the different knowledge of indigenous and Afro-descendant women and men will be highlighted.

There are two areas that require the endorsement of national authorities to ensure free, prior and informed consent (FPIC). Activities in the area of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta (SNSM) National Park involves indigenous territories through the Arhuaco and Kogui-Koguí communities. The second area is the Black Line, which includes the territory of the Kankuamo indigenous peoples, known as the Black Line. Recognized under Decree 1500 of 2016, this area is a buffer zone for the SNSM National Park and has been established to protect cultural, spiritual, cultural and environmental values. To protect the Black Line, the indigenous peoples of SNMS through the Arhuaco and Kogui authorities, are undertaking the expansion of the SNMS National Park into the Black Line territory in order to preserve their ancestral lands and the traditional management of SNMS indigenous peoples. The second area that could include indigenous territories is the San Lucas municipal area. This area includes a protected area in the San Lucas municipal. As the area of the park has not yet been delimited by the national authority, it is not possible at this time to determine whether or not there are indigenous communities active within the area.

The designation of the new protected areas is not expected to involve changes in land use and will not affect existing activities. The development of the project does not include any restrictions that should first be expressed by communities; these would be guided by a process framework and preparation of Livelihood Restoration Plans.

- Activities are consistent with national indigenous peoples' rights, as well as with FFP processes that have been undertaken with indigenous peoples and local communities at the local level to date. Ongoing activities will continue in the project area through the implementation of the project, which involves communities throughout the implementation of the project. The AE notes it will keep national indigenous organizations informed of the project development. It is also recommended that the GCF indigenous peoples focal point be available for assistance at any stage, including before a claim has been filed.

### ESSE: Cultural heritage

The project is not expected to negatively affect cultural, historical, or religious sites. The Activity-Level Eligibility and Impact Screening Form also included an assessment of the potential impact on cultural heritage (both tangible and non-tangible). While there are areas considered as cultural heritage areas in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, the project will not affect these areas and instead will promote their conservation and preservation.

### Stakeholder engagement and grievance redress mechanism

The project underwent an extensive consultation process and meetings were held at the national, regional and community levels. As a result of the identified gaps in the current policy framework, a Gender Action Plan has been prepared which summarizes the process and results of the consultations so far conducted and provides a strategic plan for the implementation phase of the project and during the project’s implementation phase, with national, regional and local stakeholders. All affected communities and relevant stakeholders shall be informed about the ESMP requirements and commitments in a timely manner through various communication channels and will be invited to submit review and comments.

The project includes the development for the development of an activity level GRM which will be available in the first six months of the implementation of project activities. This would allow project affected people, workers, or intended stakeholders to submit grievances, complaints, questions or suggestions directly to the project management unit (PMU) or the national PMU through a variety of communication channels. This is in addition to the availability of an existing All-level grievance mechanism which can be accessed by affected groups or individuals.

### 2. Gender policy

The GEF provided a gender assessment and action plan with the funding proposal and therefore meets all requirements of the GEF Gender Policy.

The programme’s approach to social and environmental safeguards includes an intergenerational gender approach, which is built on upholding the traditional knowledge and local views of women and men in communities. The programme is based on the understanding that both men and women are heterogeneous groups, and that notions of masculinity and femininity vary across different contexts (e.g., age, religion, culture, ethnicity/racial situation, age, educational level and disability) among others. Further, this particular approach takes into account the diversity within communities, including those within communities, their working environments, their position in households and society in general either at the personal or collective level. Thus, considering the socio-cultural diversity of the intervention areas, the project will ensure that women and men from indigenous communities and afro-descendants the project will highlight their differential knowledge, experiences and needs.

The project’s goal is to reduce deforestation, forest degradation, land-use changes and other threats to the paramo, montane, lowland and gallery forests in the targeted geography, thereby contributing to the conservation of biodiversity and the maintenance of ecosystem services generated through ecosystem integrity and functionality. Gender considerations have also been applied throughout the project cycle.

Colombia is a signatory to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) which was adopted in 1979 and ratified by Colombia in 1981, and in return has committed itself to eliminate discrimination against women. The country has worked to comply with CEDAW (the latest report to the CEDAW commission was in 2019). The feminist movement in Colombia has been active since the 1970s and has had a significant impact on the country, and led the promotion of women’s emancipation in various areas. The National Gender Strategy (2011-2030) is an important document that sets out the government’s commitment to gender equality as well. In addition, gender considerations are included in the National Policy for Forests; and in 2021, the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development launched a Gender Action Plan for mainstreaming in the NDC including sectoral inclusion of gender in transportation, industry, housing, mining/energy, agriculture as well as adaptation and mitigation initiatives.

70 Although the law of the country presents equality between women and men, there are still various challenges that hinder access and realization of human rights and gender equality. These include GBV in women and girls, trafficking and sexual exploitation, general poverty, lack of access to education, health services, employment and so on. The equality challenges on the legal capacity of women with disabilities and elderly women groups, as well as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender (LGBTI) communities poses yet another level of the gender intersectionality which the project will adopt in its approach—ensuring that there is wide participation of diverse stakeholders at the community level, including women and youth.

71 Regarding education disparities in the country while women and girls have access to education, they are still not able to access quality education due to poor conditions of employability and equitable wages. Research done by the National Higher Education Information System shows that there is a higher dropout rate among men than women in higher educational institutions. The gender gap in employment opportunities continues to exist despite their education. In its gender assessment, the AE states that women actively participating in the project will be involved at all levels of the project implementation from 260 meetings held; and women represent a large part of the technical personnel working in environmental projects. Women are also expected to participate in decision-making on the local level or among rural and indigenous communities. This project will ensure that these gaps are addressed and will promote gender equity in representation and local governance structures.

72 Women and youth (18-30 years) are more impacted by unemployment regardless of their education levels. The study found that women with secondary education represent 59 per cent of the national population employed in the informal sector at 59 per cent (women 60 per cent and men 49 per cent), rural areas, while youth aged between 18-29 years old represent a 35.4 per cent (52.4 per cent women and 30.7 per cent men). In both urban centres and rural areas with low population this proportion reaches 82.4 per cent (81.9 per cent women and 81.6 per cent men). The study also found that women are more likely to be employed in agriculture in conjunction with other socioeconomic variables, and that it also depends on place of residence. Women are also more likely than men to work for less than the minimum legal pay for work of equal value” to bridge the labour and wage gaps. The study also found that there are existing gender inequalities in access to credit and financial services. Women received loans at a rate of a total of 95,211 loans only 35 per cent of them benefited women and amounted to only 25.9 per cent of all loans issued by the banks. This is also reflected in the high unemployment gap issue in Colombia, especially in rural areas. These inequalities are highlighted in the gender assessment, as it how they relate to this project.

73 The assessment identified several gender equality issues in each project component and, among other things, it found that under component 1 (government structures for climate-responsible planning and implementation), there is a need to ensure that gender equality is mainstreamed under integration by including gender-responsive budgeting within the framework where each project action will be able to measure its differential impacts in terms of gender inequality. In order to strengthen women’s participation, it is recommended that women should be included as decision-makers; challenges and make recommendations on unpacking the roles played by women in the community and how they can be involved in decision-making processes and that personnel who will champion gender and inclusion should be included at the community level or among rural and indigenous communities. This project will ensure that women are involved in indigenous communities in their own language, in a way that recognizes their knowledge and empowers them.

### Risks

#### Overall proposal assessment (medium risk)

- The GCF is expected to provide a grant of USD 42 million for sustainable landscape finance that addresses financial resilience management practices, carbon sequencers and water regulation in Colombia. It will support the use of the PEF methodology to secure financial sustainability of the project.
- The total co-financing amount is expected to be USD 102 million, of which USD 69 million from the Government of Colombia and USD 33 million from the GCF will provide co-financing of USD 32 million.

#### Colombia has an investment grade rating and its fiscal track record may allow for expediting reimbursement claims from GCF. The AE has supported the full grant application, but it is not certain that the market for nature-based solutions is still resilient and not considered a bankable asset class.
- In addition to providing USD 42 million of co-financing through the PEF methodology, Colombia will provide by providing 68 per cent of the total project cost, and financing 100 per cent of costs through a carbon tax beyond the project implementation period.

#### Accredited entity/executing entity's capability to execute the current project (low risk)

- The WWF US is the AE of this project. The AE has a track record of implementing a similar PFP project financed by GCF (GFP India Bhutan for Lilac). It will provide all the GCF proceeds to the EEC and will be responsible for disbursing the funds.
- There are two EEs: Patrimonio and WWF Colombia. Patrimonio has experience in managing similar types of projects with a budget range of USD 12–98 million. WWF Colombia is an independent entity that has been working on forest conservation activities associated with the WWF US (AE). It has a track record in carrying out similar conservation activities in Colombia and has demonstrated its capacity to manage projects of this nature.
- The EEs have been pre-screened, and determined that they are capable of applying WWF US and GCF standards and policies in the execution of this project.

### 4.3.1 Project-specific execution risks (medium risk)

#### Co-financing risk
The success of project implementation rests on the suitable co-financing that will be provided from the Government of Colombia. The Government is planning to allocate at least USD 3 million per year from the carbon tax, which will be channelled through the ECF. If this co-financing does not materialize or if it is delayed, the availability of co-financing is not materialized or delayed, project implementation will be adversely affected. The term sheet includes the availability of the Government annual co-financing as a condition for disbursement of funds from the ECF. This co-financing will be disbursed on an annual basis and on throughout the project implementation.

#### Implementation risk
The project implementation period is 10 years. Consequently, the project is going to be carried out under multiple administrations with different priorities. All identified several risks relating to the regulatory environment and government policies, including changes in the carbon market, climate change, environmental expansion, and political instability. The project target areas were selected to avoid high risks of such high-level uncertainties. However, there are still some risks related to the future administrations for the political sector. Also, the GCF funds will not be received or managed by the Government.

#### Effectiveness and efficiency
The AE carried out financial and economic analyses considering adaptation co-benefits, benefits from the avoided emissions, and changes to forest carbon stocks. The analysis was conducted using a discounted cash flow model in the voluntary carbon market. The funding proposal also provides stress test scenarios where there is an increase of 50% in the price of carbon credits or a decrease of 25% in the price of carbon credits. This project will be economically and financially viable over 30 years. This is largely based on the assumption that the project will continue to receive co-financing from the Government, financial resources and that the project benefits will be sustained beyond the project implementation. This is heavily dependent on the availability of the continuous public domestic resources and additional co-financing for the project as proposed for the project.

#### Compliance risk (medium risk)

### Indicator Framework

Although the theory of change diagram does not demonstrate a differentiated approach, the accompanying narrative explains and acknowledges the variations in the deforestation drivers. The indicator framework is designed to be flexible enough to accommodate this diversity while also building on the similarities across mosaics and adopts a unified approach for protected areas and ecosystems. It includes 12 indicators that are grouped into three logical levels: project level, output level, and the logical level.

The indicator framework has been designed with relevant details as per the GCF integrated project cycle (IPC) methodology. The selected GCF result areas and BMF indicators will enable the project managers to capture and report on mitigation and adaptation outcomes. These include the following:

- Indicator 1: Project-level emissions reduced, avoided or removed/conserved.
- Indicator 2: Direct and indirect biodiversity conservation achieved.
- Indicator 3: Project-level land use change prevented.
- Indicator 4: Low-emission and/or climate-resilient management practices.
- Indicator 5: Supplementary indicator 4.1: hectares of terrestrial forest, terrestrial non-forest, freshwater and coastal marine areas brought under sustainable management.

At the GCF outcome level, the AE has strengthened the means of verification for the BMF result areas. The AE will use a combination of quantitative and qualitative indicators to combine primary and secondary data sources, and qualitative and quantitative sources where possible.

#### 1. This funding proposal for a medium-sized project in environmental and social safeguard areas is expected to have a significant impact on the proposed project contributing to both adaptation (51 per cent) and mitigation (39 per cent) results areas. The World Wildlife Fund, Inc. (WWF) is the accredited entity (AE), and the two executing entities are WWF Colombia and the National Park System of Colombia (SINAP). Heritage Colombia is a Natural Patrimonio Natural para la Biodiversidad y Areas Protegidas). The total cost of the funding proposal is US$10.2 million, with US$8.3 million as co-financing from WWF Colombia and US$1.9 million is co-finance from the Government of Colombia and WWF.

- The project's objective is to re-evaluate a new paradigm of sustainable landscape finance that enables the conservation of biodiversity in protected areas and buffer zones, sequestering and storing carbon, and generating water regulation and provisioning in a changing climate, while improving the livelihoods of vulnerable communities. The key components moving towards this objective are: (i) the improvement and implementation of governance structures for the management of landscapes; (ii) the development and implementation of early warning monitoring systems that generate climate information for improved decision-making in territorial planning and implementation of landscape restoration projects; and (iii) landscape restoration to reduce carbon emissions and strengthen the adaptive capacity of vulnerable communities.

- The project follows the same concept as a previously approved GCF project, Bhutan for Life (FP505), for which WWF-US was also the AE. It supports the project finance for permanent protection of 12 million hectares of protected areas in Bhutan, including the network of protected areas (PAs) and their buffer zones, for their biodiversity, climate change adaptation and mitigation benefits. The approach shifts a country's dependence on international and national aid to a more sustainable model that can be replicated elsewhere.

- The GCF project contributes towards the FP2 programme in Colombia called Herencia Colombia, or Heritage Colombia, which is a landscape conservation initiative designed to secure financial sustainability for large-scale landscape management by blending public, bilateral, and private sector funding. It aims at achieving shared common climate-conservation goals and deployed against a shared investment plan.

- Over the past five years, HECO's founding partners have designed an ambitious programme to protect or restore 20 million hectares (ha) over the next 20 years (increased in

# Cross-cutting impact

Some of the project’s impacts will be felt across adaptation and mitigation activities. The project is on track to make progress towards the total spatial area of 6,647,279 ha of natural resource areas to be brought under low-emissions and/or climate-resilient land use management practices (e.g., agroforestry systems, agroecology, and restoration and rehabilitation in surrounding buffer zones and connecting corridors. The project will also contribute to the strengthening of institutional capacity and engagement in institutions involved in the management of PAs and surrounding landscape mosaics by:

- Updating 64 protected area management plans to include climate change adaptation strategies.
- Strengthening 18 monitoring programs including river basin early warning systems;
- Training 150 community members and 90 public officials; and
- Fully adopting and implementing 10 governance mechanisms for the incorporation of biodiversity conservation into land use planning.

## Adaptation impact

The project aims to deliver impacts against two GCF adaptation results areas in the project mosaic:

- Increasing resilience of vulnerable communities;
- Improving resilience of ecosystems and ecosystem services (as well as livelihoods based on these).

### The funding proposal outlines the major climate change-related hazards characterizing the landscape mosaic, including drought caused by increased temperatures combined with changing rainfall patterns in some areas; and more floods and landslides caused by increasing intensity of extreme weather events. These hazards are expected to increase in frequency and severity over time.

The project proposes a series of adaptation interventions that will be implemented on the basis of observed historical trends of climate parameters, where the occurrences of both droughts and floods have increased significantly since 1980 compared with previous decades. The independent TAP notes that there has not been any seasonal attribution to the two hazards in the last three years (2015-2017) as they occurred in different seasons within the same annual water cycle. Similar lapses are found in the analysis of projected future climate in the coming decades, with no analysis of drought, using appropriate drought parameters and indices, or any assessment of the relationship between known hazards, as claimed, have not thus been analyzed and explained adequately.

### The project proposes a series of adaptation interventions that will be implemented to prevent, mitigate, and restore natural ecosystems in order to preserve or enhance the provision of key services that help buffer these climate change impacts. These interventions include maintenance of water flows to address droughts; reduction of sedimentation in rivers and lakes to maintain beneficial flows and from increasingly extreme rainfall events; and reduction of localized and downstream flooding.

The project will also contribute to the restoration of degraded ecosystems, including:

- 329,658 inhabitants of the project mosaic will be direct beneficiaries benefiting from the ecosystem-based adaptation interventions across 6,602 ha in protected areas and 945.1 ha in buffer zones.
- Of the direct beneficiaries, 3,618 small-scale farmers in eight locations will also benefit from the implementation of climate-smart agriculture practices that build-on farm resilience to increasing extremes (and reduce pressures on surrounding ecosystems).


---
**Page 226**
---

A total of 19,443,108 people, representing 53 per cent of the total population, will benefit indirectly from interventions protecting and maintaining the 6.6 million hectares of project mosaic ecosystems that provide critical resilience benefits, including water regulation, flood protection, and erosion control.

The adaptation impact of the project, while expected to be significant, may be challenging to measure. The funding proposal states that adaptation benefits to indirect beneficiaries will be measured through changes in ecosystem services (e.g., water regulation, flood protection, and erosion control) and land use change resulting from improved governance, PA management, and restoration and rehabilitation interventions.

The project seeks to deliver greenhouse gas emissions reduction and removals of 1.3 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (t CO2eq) in 10 years, and 46.3 million tCO2eq from reduced deforestation, forest restoration and preservation of land cover over the lifetime of the project.

The estimation of reductions and removals is based on the difference between the projected emissions with and without the project interventions across all scenarios falling into three categories, as shown in annex 2A: (i) carbon removal as a result of restoration and rehabilitation; (ii) existing carbon stocks and links sought under more

## 1.2 Paradigm shift potential Scale: Medium to high

The proposed project is designed to bring about two significant paradigm shifts. The first shift is one from reliance on piecemeal donor funding to plug-in gas to state financing of Colombia’s forests and their associated ecosystem services. This represents a transition to long-term financial sustainability through public-private partnerships and dedicated long-term domestic revenue sources. The second major aspect of paradigm shift can be seen in the project’s approach to forest governance, which is designed to ensure that they can continue to deliver critical services for decades to come, in the face of evolving political and economic conditions. This will require a significant degree of independence from the success of government’s efforts, through this and other initiatives, to secure lasting peace and stability in Colombia. The project seeks to achieve these goals through effective and humane law enforcement combined with planned integral rural reform.

### 1.2 Project Finance for Permanence Approach

The HECO PFP approach is strongly aligned with GCF principles of permanence and sustainability. The HECO PFP vision is about using upfront funds during a transition period to create the conditions to access long-term financing from public-private partnerships, as well as domestic sources. With the initial investment of the GCF funds and co-finance, this project seeks to increase the baseline of forest cover in Colombia by 2030 by 15 million hectares (Mha). The use of GCF funds will attract an additional USD 162.2 million in new investment as direct co-finance into these landscapes from WWF, the Government of Colombia and various philanthropic donors over the next decade. This is expected to generate a total economic value of USD 305.8 million, which would be translated into USD 8.2 million in annual recurring budget allocations to the HEC (the existing baseline, shown above, is based on the current GCF project).

The proposed GCF project forms a crucial part of the wider HEDO partnership. A public ceremony was held in Bogotá, Colombia on 8 December 2015 to mark the signing of the donors and partners on the PFP's conservation plan and financial model, totalling USD 245 million’s worth of planned activities. This funding will support the creation, expansion and improvement of protected areas (PAs) in Colombia, covering approximately 37 million ha, so that 26 per cent of Colombia’s land territory and 30 per cent of its oceans will be under protection. Facilitation funds from the GCF are being used to support the PFP implementation phase. The initial initiative (whose funds are managed through WWF), shown in orange in the diagram above (left) is the Amazon Region Protected Areas Program (ARPA). Other partners include: Pre- Trustee Charitable, Wildlife Conservation Society, World Bank, European Union, Inter-American Development Bank, and GCF.

The HEDO partnership also aims to lock in the permanent protection of about 13 per cent of the entire Amazon rainforest, in concert with PFP initiatives under way or planned in Brazil and Peru. The PFP approach is a new model for financing conservation that has been developed by building on global experiences with the PFP approach: Amazon Region Protected Areas (ARPA) Program in Brazil, the World Bank’s Forest Carbon Partnership Facility (FCPF), and the Bhutan Biodiversity and Life Initiative, of which the GCF Bhutan for Life project (FPP05) forms the cornerstone. Since these projects are still ongoing, it is too early for a rigorous evaluation of their results, but they have been successful in demonstrating that PFPs can be an effective mechanism to attract donor funds, and over USD 600 million in domestic financial commitments, to preserve over 70 million ha of tropical forest. The GCF has now committed to supporting the development of the PFP approach in Amazon countries, including the ARPA Program in Brazil, published a guide to the PFP approach, which highlights some key features of PFPs which make it a new and powerful approach to biodiversity and climate financing.

### Gender benefits

Although not specifically highlighted in section D.3 of the funding proposal, the project’s gender strategy includes a range of activities aimed at improving women’s access to land and other assets. For example, it notes that 35.7 per cent of rural women (compared with only 7.8 per cent of rural men) do not have their own income, and about 20 per cent of female-headed households are food-insecure. The project will also seek to address any other areas of inequality, including lower access to land ownership, to credit and financial inclusion, to community decision-making processes, and to the provision of social services. Women’s vulnerability in the face of climate-related events such as droughts or floods, many rural women prioritizing their own food security over that of their families, and the lack of sufficient food for household consumption; all these activities are highly impacted by climate-related events, placing women at greater risk than men.

The project will include a training programme with departmental and municipal institutions on gender responsive and socially inclusive action plans. Governance schemes involving local communities will be strengthened to ensure that they have a strong and intergenerational focus to improve dialogue. This will include strengthening the capacity of local community-based organizations (CBOs) for change, incorporating indigenous knowledge and gender responsiveness. Ten selection committees responsible for allocating land will develop an organizational development plan to enhance social and gender inclusion, while co-developing strategies with women’s groups to ensure that they have access to project resources. A differential gender and intergenerational approach will also be taken to participate in the design of climate change adaptation strategies to make sure the groups of young people and women in each landscape.

# 1.4 Needs of the recipient

## Scale: High

### Colombia is vulnerable to extreme weather impacts, with a high recurrence and magnitude associated with changing climate conditions.

The country is recognized as vulnerable to the impacts of climate change due to a combination of socio-political and geographical factors. Colombia has been ranked in the top 10 most vulnerable countries by the Global Adaptation Initiative (ND-GAIN) Index. Although Colombia is an upper middle-income country with some positive economic indicators and trends, it has high levels of inequality, with a Gini coefficient of 54.2% in 2019. The country also faces significant poverty challenges: nearly half of the population lives below the poverty line. The country has made progress in recent years in developing climate change adaptation strategies, but there is still much to be done.

### Although Colombia has a national climate financing strategy and a new tax reform law has just been passed to increase revenues, including through the carbon tax, the country still lacks a comprehensive framework for climate change adaptation. The government needs additional resources for addressing this challenge.

# Country ownership

## Policy and strategy alignment

The project is well aligned with a set of key national commitments, policies and strategies related to climate change, biodiversity and combating deforestation. The GCF project contributes directly to Colombia’s National Climate Change Strategy (NCCS), which sets out the country's contributions towards Colombia's efforts to implement/achieve these at the heart of these commitments are the following: the 2015 Paris Agreement, which commits Colombia to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 20 million ha (recently increased to 32 million ha), the Heritage Colombia initiative, first announced in 2014 and now part of the National Climate Change Strategy, and the Paris Convention on Climate Change in 2015. This wider HEICO initiative, of which the GCF project forms a part, aims at reducing deforestation by 36% (from 7 million ha to 4.5 million ha) in Colombia’s NDCs (revised in 2020) which aim to reduce national greenhouse gas emissions by 51 per cent against the baseline by 2030, with the agriculture, forestry, and other land use sector of the economy contributing approximately 68% of total GHG emissions. Colombia’s NDCs target a reduction in deforestation rates from an average of 479,000 ha/year in 2012, reaching 100,000 ha/year by 2025 and 50,000 ha per year by 2030.

The project also contributes to Colombia’s National Forest Strategy (CONFENIFOR No. 46/21), which defines a 2030 goal to achieve zero net deforestation through the implementation of four strategies to which the GCF project contributes directly: promoting sustainable forest management; ## Engagement with civil society

Engagement with civil society organizations, including with indigenous peoples and Afro-descendant communities, has been ongoing since the initial design phase of the project. This engagement is based on principles of free, prior, and informed consent and prior consultation, as well as the application of WWF's social and environmental safeguards framework.

### Landscape approach

The landscape approach is being used to integrate conservation with development in country initiatives and uses domestic systems to ensure accountability. Also, by taking a landscape approach, it is possible to address multiple objectives at once, including adaptation, aligning policies and land-planning instruments, and implementing coordinated actions between governments, private sector, civil society in SINAP and other environmentally strategic actors.

### Response to a query

In response to a query from the independent TAP about involvement of the domestic private sector in the project, WWF Colombia has identified four areas of engagement related to the long-term financing strategy through the carbon tax, and the SGR paid for private sector exploitation of non-renewable natural resources: (i) the involvement of smallholder farmers leading to the development of a market for their products; (ii) the creation of new local markets; (iii) the inclusion in the project design of support to pipeline development for the Amazon basin, which will be linked with the expansion of the supply chain for tropical fruits and cotonutus; (iv) the project's support to a digital platform for sustainable Amazon products that will be developed together with WWF Colombia and the American Development Bank partners.

### Response to questions from the independent TAP

In response to questions from the independent TAP about risks involved in providing financing through the private sector, given its significant role in deforestation across the Amazon biome, and the potential to link with national and global initiatives to monitor and reduce deforestation, WWF Colombia has identified four areas of engagement on the commercial chain. The A highlighted the adoption in 2012 by the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (MADR) of a new law for Bosque y Rurales species, to be implemented in conjunction with the government's new national policy on sustainable cattle ranching.

### Country ownership

The country ownership of the project is thus seen to be high.


## Efficiency and effectiveness

### Scale: High

In terms of potential to catalyze and/or leverage investment, the proposed project is impressive. The scale of the project, together with the project finance for performance-based payments means that the Government of Colombia, with a broad coalition of community, public sector, and private sector philanthropic partners, are able to demonstrate their commitment to long-term conservation strategies and goals.

### Project proposal budget

Of the project's total proposed budget of USD 14.5 million, only 30 per cent (USD 4.3 million) is covered by a GCF grant, and 70 years (USD 10.2 million) is made up of government and WWF co-financing to the project. The USD 69.8 million in co-finance from the Government of Colombia is directly linked with the direct implementation of the GCF conservation plan, and are also project activities within the proposed GCF project's logical framework. This is above and beyond government's routine contributions to the current

baseline funding for protected areas. During the project’s 10-year window, GCF funds will unlock USD 38.2 million in new investment, committed as direct co-finance into these landscapes by WWF-US and various philanthropic donors whose funds are channeled through WWF-US.

62. The project's proposed 100 per cent concessionality level is justiﬁed because it is investing in ecosystem goods and services that are public in nature, such as water provision from the Amazon Basin to the Caribbean Sea, and the maintenance of biodiversity across the region. The project invests in landscape mosaics at the core of which are public assets, in the form of national parks and protected areas. These assets provide a range of ecosystem goods and services infrastructure and capacity; the ongoing costs of maintaining these systems will be funded from revenues generated by the project’s activities, following the GCF’s 100 per cent concessionality approach. Where GCF funds will be used to support small-scale farmers, the proﬁts to be derived from climate-resilient agricultural practices in a very small scale will accrue directly to vulnerable and poor households, part of building resilience against future environmental shocks and stresses, including those caused by climate change.

63. The project is designed as an integrated landscape approach sustainable in order to achieve the proposal’s objectives. GCF grant funding is the anchor of a coherent package of grant financing from the Colombian Government, other multilateral and bilateral donors and private philanthropic donors. This package includes both direct co-ﬁnancing (GCF grants), concessionally equivalent amount among all co-financers. Landscapes that integrate networks of protected areas with community-managed lands and other land uses provide multiple ecosystem services and climate beneﬁts to local, national and global communities. While this project will deliver beneﬁts for the entire region, it is particularly important in Colombia because those most vulnerable to climate change – those most directly reliant on natural resources for their livelihoods – are the principal beneﬁciaries of these landscape investments.

64. The proposal combines an ecosystem-based mitigation and adaptation approach, which considers the improved management of forest ecosystems in and around protected areas to reduce carbon emissions from deforestation and degradation (component 1), increasing economic returns to communities (component 3). Direct economic costs of managing protected areas, buffer zones and connectivity corridors will be offset by increased revenues from timber sales, ecotourism, and rotational livestock production, and up to USD 153,118,927. Economic beneﬁts from mitigation (avoided emissions), adaptation (avoided losses in climate regulation services like water provision and regulation of the hydrological cycle) and increased economic returns for communities increasing water supply variability and weather extremes add up to USD 1,225,032,458.

65. Analysis shows that the project has a net present value (NPV) above USD 9 billion, an inﬁnite economic internal rate of return (IRR) and a net present value (NPV) above USD 1 trillion, reﬂecting the enormous value of Colombia’s forests for climate regulation. In addition, the development of a new enhanced climate information system will provide signiﬁcant adaptation beneﬁts by providing real-time early warning information on weather hazards to help reduce crop losses and livestock mortality in the region. The NPV of this component is USD 16,900,689 and the economic internal rate of return (IRR) is 25 per cent with a net present value above USD 3 billion. The enhanced climate information system will have an economic cost of USD 16,700,689 and the total project NPV for this component is USD 4,200,000. The internal rate of return (IRR) is 13 per cent, and a net-present value of USD 17,155,051. Both component 3 and the net present value above USD 9 billion, reﬂecting the enormous value of Colombia’s forests for climate regulation. For the full project, the NPV is higher than USD 1 trillion, reﬂecting its extremely high role that Colombian tropical forests have for their role in climate regulation. This result is underpinned by the fact that the project has a very low discount rate.

66. The ﬁnancial analysis for private beneﬁciaries shows ﬁnancial viability of the project interventions of rehabilitation schemes that include sustainable production systems and on-


---
**Page 239**
---

farm support for climate adaptation. The cost-benefit analysis completed for activities 3.1.1 and 3.2.1 – the implementation of sustainable and climate-adapted agroforestry and silvopastoral production systems in combination with additional on-farm adaptation support – shows the GCF’s investment in these projects will generate USD 4,058 per hectare over a 20-year time horizon. This would also increase from 11 to 32 percent. While traditional production schemes prove not to be financially viable under climate change stress scenarios, the project interventions based on sustainable and climate-adapted agroforestry and silvopastoral production schemes in the project area reveal a positive financial return.

Test scenarios for the private beneficiaries prove that project interventions with GCF support in the form of grants stay financially viable even if the situation of cost increases or revenue decreases. The net present value (NPV) generated by the project over a 20-year time horizon will be USD -1,825,349 with a financial internal rate of return (FIRR) of 6 percent and an NPV yield ratio of 7.5 percent or more than double the FIRR relative to the without-project scenario under traditional production.

The cost-effectiveness of the GCF’s investment in achieving the project's mitigation benefits can be seen in the estimated cost per tCO2 eq, which is just USD 3.14 per tCO2 eq (defined as the amount of CO2 equivalent emissions avoided or sequestered).

The project's overall efficiency and effectiveness is rated as high.

### Overall remarks from the Independent Technical Advisory Panel

The independent TAP believes this public sector project from the Government of Colombia, implemented by IDEAM, has a strong potential to contribute to Colombia’s efforts towards effective management and sustainable financing of protected area landscapes that play a vital role in climate change mitigation. The TAP recommends that the GCF recommend to the AfT that they undertake the following in the project inception phase:

- Seek clarity on the planned relationship between the new FONAFIFO fund, established in terms of Law 1709 (effective from January 2023) and the existing fund (effective December 2021), receive the national carbon tax proceeds, and the flow and tracking of funds for the HEEDCO project.
- Put in place agreements between IDEAM, the National Parks Agency, relevant research institutions and local communities for monitoring, reporting and verification of reduced emissions from deforestation and forest degradation (REDD+), as well as their rights and responsibilities, as well as systems and methods for data collection and reporting.

The independent TAP endorses the funding proposal for the project "Heritage Colombia (HEEDCO)" under the GCF’s 2019-2023 Strategic Plan, subject to the following conditions being met prior to the first GCF disbursement:

- Delivery by the Accredited Entity to the GCF, in a form and substance satisfactory to the GCF Secretariat, of a plan for the operation and maintenance of all of the infrastructure and components financed under this project, including any co-financiers as part of the Funded Activity (the "Operations and Maintenance Plan").
